proton beam's beam current. Furthermore, the minimal acceptable signal-to-nois 
threshold for employing this method in the AWAKE experiment has been found to 
be around 0.1% in the proton beam current precision, which is a condition 
easily met given the high-quality conditions of the AWAKE experiment's 
equipment.

Recent advances in differentially private machine learning (DMPL) have led to the development of several learning algorithms, although many of these solutions primarily address linear models. To bridge this gap, this research focuses on creating reliable, differentially private decision tree learning methodologies. Existing solutions in this domain either severely compromise on privacy or excessively limit the usable data. Building upon a previously established approach for locally differentially private decision tree learning, this research tackles the challenge of a central party learning decision trees in a distributed setting. By addressing this problem, our proposed algorithm ensures that only the final learned trees, not the underlying training data, are visible to the central party, thus maintaining differential privacy. Furthermore, our technique allows for the utilization of nearly all data samples in the distributed setting, resulting in statistically reliable learning. When compared to a recent algorithm for differentially private decision tree learning in a central party setting, our method maintains comparable accuracy while ensuring that only the final learned trees, not the underlying data, are visible to the central party, thus maintaining differential privacy.

We introduce a family of regularized entropy-based divergence metrics that incorporate prior knowledge in unsupervised clustering problems. These generalized divergences, inspired by the Kullback-Leibler and R\'enyi families, are shown to have consistent finite-sample performance guarantees. To estimate these generalized divergences, we develop a method using the Bregman proximal gradient approach, which is an efficient algorithm showing linear convergence. We validate the effectiveness of our approach in clustering tasks across various datasets.

CEGs are versatile models that describe variable relationships, used across various fields including quality control, healthcare, and safety research. In many cases, multiple CEGs representing the same phenomenon can be envisioned. This paper proposes an approach to identify the most suitable model among alternatives based on data analysis. It combines model selection and parameter estimation in a single Bayesian framework, introducing an auxiliary variable to account for model variations. The method is demonstrated on real-world accident data, specifically on a dataset related to off-shore workers.

In the context of finding the minimal norm solution in forward problems, a new inertial process with zero regularization is proposed. Building on the conventional dynamical system used in the case of non-zero and vanishing Tikhonov regularization, the net motion under the given system is now purely deterministic and no longer subject to random influences that might impede convergence. With a focus on the system lacking a equilibrium or having a minimally stable minimizer, a comprehensive examination of the system's long-term behavior is performed. Consequently, it has been determined that in the system lacking a equilibrium or having a minimally stable minimizer, the trajectory is directed towards the minimizer with the minimal norm, with convergence taking place at a rate not exceeding O(Δt^(1/2)).

This paper marks a departure from typical finite-time convergence methods in
robotics by investigating unpredictable behavior in a simple task. We examine
a scenario where a robot is designed to follow a moving wall, with a
proportionate control law that steers it towards the wall's lead point. Our
analysis, employing geometric methods on an extended phase space, reveals that
under specific conditions, the system exhibits chaotic behavior, characterized
by infinite derivative blowup and unpredictable trajectory shifts. A phase
space decomposition allows us to quantify these shifts, which are shown to be
completely unpredictable and randomly distributed, a first such instance of
uncontrolled motion in a robotic system.

Within the framework of a model that explains superconductivity through a drive in intensity, we investigated and analyzed how high-frequency electromagnetic radiation interacts with cuprate superconductors that have been altered, through a process known as doping. Utilizing the Zinser-Franke formalism, we calculated how the presence of defects impacted the response of these superconductors to microwave radiation, specifically their attenuation, at various energy levels and in relation to their composition. We discovered that, in the superconducting state, these alterations result in distinct patterns of change, and that, in the normal state, the strength of this response is directly related to the frequency of the microwave radiation and the extent to which the superconductor has been altered. Moreover, we observed that, in both states, the presence of extended types of defects significantly affect the absorption of microwave radiation, leading to increased transmission and thus less absorption, at low frequencies while, on the contrary, the absorption is increased at high frequencies and in regions where the frequency is roughly equivalent to the drive frequency and the frequency of oscillation within the superconductor. These findings demonstrate that, in these materials, the absorption of microwave radiation is a complex function of numerous variables including frequency, doping levels, and the presence of extended defects which in turn are linked with the frequency of the external drive. Additionally, these results emphasize the significance of exploring absorption, rather than transmission, when examining cuprate superconductors that have been altered through a process known as doping

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow. A comprehensive review of this topic is provided, focusing on the initial value problem's solvability and well-definedness.

A notable achievement in training reinforcement learning agents lies in successfully guiding plants through the process of elongation, particularly during the geotropic growth phase that enables plants to correctly orient their roots in relation to gravity's direction, ensuring optimal root development in limited spaces and preventing overextension. This research involves training a neural agent within the GrowSpace environment, where the objective is to maximize rewards by promoting geotropic root growth while avoiding overgrowth through novel combined methods of root guidance and root reinforcement learning, training agents in tandem, and incorporating an environment enrichment strategy that applies rotating barriers to stimulate bending roots and creating opportunities for exploration and optimization.

We demonstrate how to utilize the conformal field theory of quantum disks in the discrete spin partition to calculate the critical ising field and determine SLE loop equations, and subsequently verify that the resulting observables resemble Schram-Postnikov polynomials. Additionally, we outline a method for computing the partition function of the ising model on a pyramid-like structure in the discrete spin partition. This approach involves adapting the quantum disk's conformal field theory. Such a method can also be applied to similar problems in general central charges.

The Image Biomarker Analysis Affinity Group consists of biomedical imaging researchers, who through extensive discussion and presentation of specific methods, have established a comprehensive framework for reporting imaging biomarker analysis results. This standard involves providing detailed information regarding image acquisition and analysis processing, as well as quantifying biomarker performance and evaluating the impact of evaluation sample composition and size. A key concept is the 'effective number of samples', which accounts for the influence of imbalance and size on binary classification tasks. A software tool, 'ebayes', has been developed to automate the analysis, facilitating reproducible and transparent imaging biomarker research. This project's finding are accessible at the URL: https://github.com/ibis-image-biomarkers/IBNI

We examine the dynamic nature of $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction on the nucleon, taking into consideration a unique type of nucleon resonance with a high spin value. It's well established that isoscalar photons induce significant low-spin nucleon resonances but leave little impact on high-spin resonances, whereas isovector photons have a pronounced effect on high-spin resonances while being minimal for low-spin ones. Consequently, the high-spin nature of nucleon resonances is primarily influenced by isovector photons. Furthermore, we investigate how high-spin excitations of the nucleon affect $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction, in addition to exploring the potential role of the delta resonance in these interactions. It's essential to consider that high-spin resonances, mainly influenced by isovector photons, manifest distinctly in $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction. On the other hand, a prominent delta excitation, which receives little input from isoscalar photons, can significantly impact both $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction. Notably, a recent experiment set against the background of a sea of nucleon resonances has collected essential data, struggling to identify prominent low-spin resonances while uncovering potential high-spin excitations, which are in line with our hypothesis that high-spin nucleon resonances and delta excitations play a crucial role in $K\Lambda$ and

For effective cross-cultural and cross-racial facial recognition research, it is essential to have diverse datasets. The OpenFace benchmark, utilized in this study, requires standardized input images. Typically, image preparation involves using a data enhancement tool, but this process can be time-consuming and prone to errors. We present a morphables II collection preparation method leveraging the OpenCV toolkit's efficiency and accuracy, significantly reducing preparation time to nearly an hour, down from the previous 644 hours. Moreover, our images are fully extractable and adjustable in resolution. The provided code extracts morpables II faces at 46x45 resolution, totaling 2764 images, accompanied by corresponding standardization transformations, facilitating training within the OpenFace framework.

We suggest that the dark matter component, other than the primordial black holes, might be entirely or largely made up of a type of incompressible dark medium, hypothetically existing at an early stage of the universe. Within the framework of the 'running curvaton' model, where the dark medium acts as a curvaton, we investigate the generation of dark matter in the form of incompressible fluid. This model incorporates two key factors: the quantum gravity-driven variation in the dark medium's mass, implemented through the dilaton-Photon mixing, and a symmetrical breaking of the gauge group 2U(1). Our computations reveal how these factors affect the mass variation range of the dark medium and the resulting mass range of the primordial black holes, which could account for all or a significant portion of dark matter within this scenario.

The analysis of academic pathways has been gaining traction, with a focus on understanding school choices that lead to specific career outcomes, such as PhD or law professionals. Previous research has utilized single latent variable models to establish career and educational trajectories. However, this study advocates for the use of models that incorporate multiple latent variables to account for varying academic pursuits within a single occupation. Specifically, we employ a model-based clustering method to analyze a dataset of academic employees in the US, based on data from the National Science Foundation's Survey of College and University Employment. This model allows us to categorize employees into distinct clusters based on their educational backgrounds, while controlling for occupational variations. By comparing two model variants with an existing association model, we find that a model-based clustering approach yields more compact representations and better captures inter-units variations, making it more suitable for analyzing academic-to-career trajectories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a single latent variable model-based clustering approach is capable of producing classifications that closely resemble those from an association model, while also offering the advantage of identifying distinct sub-clusters within a single occupation.

To increase efficiency on highways with a high percentage of automated and
self-driving vehicles, we are exploring a new control strategy. This strategy
involves organizing pre-planned vehicle clusters upon the initial connection of
successive self-driving vehicles. Our approach uses a game theory concept called
Differential Dynamic Programming to optimize and arrange these vehicle clusters
based on their current and anticipated positions, velocities, and time of arrival.
By incorporating this clustering strategy, we aim to reduce the time it takes for
successive self-driving vehicles to get closer to each other and prepare them for
traveling at a closer distance, thereby improving the performance and safety of
the highway. Furthermore, Arrangement Control, another game theory concept, is
used to set a target spacing for the vehicle clusters based on their current and
anticipated states, and this spacing is utilized to calculate control strategies
for the vehicle clusters. We have proven the robustness of the vehicle cluster
planning and arranged spacing through an analysis under various assumptions.
Moreover, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach through a time
paradigm analysis and evaluated its performance using real-world data and an
environment simulation.

Interactions are a crucial aspect of predictive models, influencing how well they perform. In the absence of interactions, gradient boosting algorithms operate independently with each tree, based on previous trees. However, when interactions are present, there's a problem: algorithms can't guarantee convergence. Economists have used gradient descent for centuries, particularly in the method of least squares, and recent breakthroughs in derivative-free optimization have led to a surge in demand for derivatives. We've discovered a way to apply the categorical CatBoost algorithm, originally without interactions, to models involving interactions, by utilizing gradients based on past results. This approach offers a straightforward solution, avoiding the need for modified algorithms or approximations. We've developed a straightforward method to calculate gradients based on past results, along with an optimal number of recent results needed for convergence. This approach also offers an interesting interpretation, similar to surrogate gradient approaches from optimization theory, especially relevant for experts in convex optimization who may not be familiar with the field. This innovation has significant real-world implications, especially in situations where data is expensive or costly to obtain, and in the use of online learning, where data is constantly evolving. In addition, we've explored a variant of surrogate gradients, offering the potential for even more efficient interactions. However, this variant also offers a challenge: how to determine an optimal surrogate gradient, and what guarantees it offers for convergence in the most general case?

Our research focuses on determining the effectiveness of mechanically created headlines in distinguishing themselves from original stories. In this study, we utilize two large datasets, MCH-15 and MCH-19, which contain samples collected in 2015 and 2019, to evaluate the accuracy of various models, including those based on CNN, LSTM, and transformer architectures. Notably, our experiments using the BERT model and different fusion strategies with multiple models reveal that mechanically created headlines can be distinct from original stories.

The study of materials with topological properties, especially those containing exotic quantum entities like the chiral spin liquid, has been particularly difficult due to the lack of a clear guiding principle for their synthesis. We suggest that both amorphous and polycrystalline methods can be used to produce such rare materials, which we define as "hetero-crystalline compounds." By merging concepts from theoretical models and experimental frameworks, we explore how merging two topological materials with different crystal structures can lead to the creation of chiral spin liquids. Focusing on chiral topological insulators and superconductors, we explain how combining them with a heavy metal in three different ways can result in a non-magnetic state with unique properties. Using a theoretical model and by solving a complex equation, we analyze the interplay of electronic interactions and spin-orbit effects that can give rise to this atypical state. We further validate this prediction using a complex network of theoretical and experimental methods, including the study of electronic properties, the influence of crystalline defects, the possible emergence of local moments, and the interference of magnetic impurities with the spin of quantum entities.

The increasing interest in large-scale radio interferometers, particularly in exoplanet research, is driving a need for more efficient methods to accurately calibrate their operations. These interferometers, consisting of multiple antennas collecting data on a regular grid, face calibration challenges that traditionally require higher computational resources as the number of antennas grows. In this work, we present a novel calibration technique leveraging the grid structure, transforming the traditional computationally complex problem into one with a much lower requirement for large-N systems. This method adapts to regular grids behind firewalls and is demonstrated to work effectively with standard radio interferometer data, offering an improved solution. The development of this novel approach addresses a long-standing limitation, opening up new possibilities for large-scale radio interferometers to participate in exoplanet research.

Investment returns on equities are often correlated, leading to a scenario where a portfolio may become overdiversified when too many securities are included. In our research, we investigate an underdiversified portfolio approach, starting with a comprehensive market consisting of many securities, and gradually reduce the number of holdings to achieve improved diversification and investment outcomes, as measured by risk and return metrics. A novel automatic feature extraction method, based on an infoGAN, is presented to determine an optimal portfolio size. To ensure the generated portfolios are both diverse and representative, a divergent markov chain is integrated into the model as a regularization technique. Furthermore, a conditional variant of the autoencoding infoGAN is introduced, enabling the identification of securities that contribute little to the reduction of the portfolio's risk, as determined by a specific risk metric such as value-at-risk. The proposed method is applied to real-world data and analyzed through experimentations, providing valuable insights into its capabilities. The study includes an in-depth examination of the subject matter, accompanied by accompanying materials including source code, data sets, and demonstration videos, available at: https://github.com/thashimiazmat/InfoGAN-analysis/tree/main/AD-InfoGAN-paper.

We have derived the polarized long-distance contributions to the massless three-loop Afg(N) function with general flavor indices f, including contributions from the regions f > 5, f = 4, f = 3, f = 2, and f = 1. To achieve this, we integrated the associated irreducible four-loop functions involving four massive flavors f, f, f', and W, where W can be 1 or 2. We also calculated the corresponding four-loop massive anomalous dimension of the operator Q_w(n, μ) and obtained the results in terms of the functions A_w(n).

Accurate classification of gamma-ray sources is a complex task, handled by the Fermi-LAT team who maintain a comprehensive catalog of gamma-ray emitters, which includes diverse astronomical objects including blazars. Employing the latest breakthroughs in machine learning architecture, specifically Bayesian artificial networks, this study endeavors to separate blazars from the Fermi-LAT catalog, focusing on distinguishing between different blazar subcategories. Leveraging the previously proven effectiveness of Bayesian artificial networks in multi-dimensional data analysis and their capacity to provide confidence levels and uncertainty margins, this study aims to offer a reliable classification framework. Moreover, additional machine learning techniques, including the application of Moon pool for selecting samples from the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray catalog, is introduced to facilitate the workflow. A thoroughly validated method is presented to disjointly classify blazars according to their subtypes and to differentiate between spine and jet regions in extended jets, validating the results with independently curated samples.

Our social media usage is primarily defined by the content creation component, 
yet numerous technological hurdles continue to hinder this process, particularly 
from a mobile perspective, such as the limitations on uploading a single image at a time. 

On the other hand, advancements in Artificial Intelligence and enhanced network infrastructure 
are paving the way for a seamless experience, such as high-quality multi-image uploads and 
engaging, personalized content suggestions that capitalize on AI. 

Ultimately, it is crucial for users to be able to leverage these capabilities on their preferred devices, 
and this presents a unique opportunity for innovative content creation that caters to human emotions and individuality.

A hypergraph is an extension of the graph concept, featuring edges that connect more than two vertices, allowing the definition of a hypergraph's tensor product, a higher-dimensional equivalent of graph products. We investigate spectral properties of hypergraphs, including a new method to calculate their Laplacian's eigenvalues, as well as patterns in these eigenvalues, and how these may relate to the hypergraph's structural organization.

The Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) proposal aims to establish a dedicated space-based observatory focused on visible to near-infrared spectroscopy and imaging.  The proposed mission includes developing a 4-m diameter telescope that would be placed in an Earth orbit or on the L2, with the primary scientific objectives being:  (1) to investigate the fundamental properties of stars and their evolution, (2) to explore the physical conditions and activities of protostars and young stars, and their influence on early solar system formation, (3) to study the fundamental properties and evolution of nearby galaxies, active galaxies, and their impact on their environment, and cosmic evolution in general, and (4) to explore the fundamental properties of the cosmos, including observations of high-z galaxies during the reionization period, and near-infrared and far-infrared observations of stars, galactic formation, and cosmic evolution.  The report includes recommendations for further development, with the caveat that a final decision on the L2 vs. Earth orbit is yet to be made.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the analysis is often compromised by death or withdrawal of some patients, resulting in missing values that can cause an issue. In such cases, the traditional approach of analyzing censored data may not be sufficient, as it can lead to misleading conclusions on treatment effectiveness for most patients. However, this problem can be resolved through the use of non-linear models that reflect the natural progression of these diseases over time. We suggest a category of parametric models grounded in probability theory, such as the log-normal Pearson model, which take into account the natural progression of the disease and how likely it is to survive without progression. Despite its effectiveness, this approach still has its limitations, as it relies heavily on pre-made formulas. To address this, we suggest using a combination of non-linear models based on natural cubic splines, which allow for a more in-depth examination and flexible adjustment of model components; hence resulting in better capture of natural disease progression course and survival curves. This model can handle a wide variety of different treatment effects on disease progression and patient survival by combining different model components. We present a dual approach, combining analysis of survival using a combination of analysis of disease progression and model analysis of survival, using a combination of analysis of disease progression and model analysis of survival. We demonstrate this approach in two real-world scenarios, including data from a study on donepezil and rivastigmine.

Our approach for analyzing complex systems, imES, has been applied to a simple model system, the two-dimensional XY magnet. This method, which is based on the configuration of configuration-space itineraries, captures distinct pathways of phase transitions. By capturing both local and global patterns of phase transitions, imES has been found to provide a comprehensive understanding of various phases and transitions. Furthermore, this method has been shown to offer a clear pathway for achieving precise control and efficient manipulation of transitions.

This discussion revolves around a system of equations that combine the properties of the Monge-Ampere equation and Hessian inequalities, specifically applicable to compact connnected domains in complex n-dimensional space. By employing a combination of the Aleksandrov Maximum Principle and a previously developed local estimate for (p, q)-Hessian equations, we establish and demonstrate the validity of a key differential inequality, ultimately leading to the derivation of Carnot's theorem for biharmonic functions in connection with this investigation.

In the context of the theory of typed lambda-calculi, a growing literature explores the relationship between type systems and limitations on computational processes. This research is primarily rooted in evidence suggesting that type systems can capture important boundaries, as illustrated by the regular functions, which serve as a fundamental concept in theoretical computer science. The features of regular functions, first identified by Kolmogorov, are synonymous with relative computability. This study expands the definition of regular functions to higher-order computability, presenting two distinct notions based on different assessment methods. It is demonstrated that these higher-order regular functions have inherent properties and that they form a closed class of functions, similar to the untyped lambda-calculus. The paper also explores the intersection of these higher-order regular functions with respect to type systems. The results indicate that the majority of non-exponential functions are not regular, providing an explication for an existing result stating that the limited domain fails to include regular functions. Conversely, a type system incorporating domain restrictions does capture the regular functions, and the paper delves into the optimal parameters for such a type system.

This note addresses the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when used with functional integrations that involve conditional flow processes of differential laws depending on underlying Wiener processes.

A new method is introduced to define the geometric property known as hyperbolicity for a subset of a Euclidean space. This method utilizes a distinct definition of intersection numbers within the context of a standard framework space, a mathematical concept developed by the same authors. The standard framework space itself is derived from the collection of all directed line segments within the Euclidean space, measured as the endpoints approach infinity. By leveraging this approach, the study demonstrates that certain embedded submanifolds in Euclidean space, characterized as having bounded intersection numbers, are indeed embedded in their corresponding standard framework space. Consequently, this reveals new classes of embedded submanifolds that are now understood to be embedded in a certain mathematical space, known as WH spaces, including submanifolds that are minimally exponentially embedded. A specific example is provided to illustrate that the embedded submanifolds that are minimally exponentially embedded do, in fact, exhibit distinct geometric properties when compared to those that are minimally embedded. Additionally, this research develops a distinct mapping, known as the Gauss map, in the context of standard framework spaces, and uses it to prove that certain embedded submanifolds, characterized as having a certain mathematical property known as negative curvature, are in fact embedded in their corresponding spaces, as demonstrated through a specific example.

This study focuses on cross-domain text-to-SQL, aiming to convert input natural language to SQL queries with relevant tables. A major obstacle in text-to-SQL systems is understanding linguistic patterns in user queries. In our research, we present a cutting-edge method using auxiliary tasks to enhance linguistic analysis across domains. An auxiliary task models is integrated with the text-to-SQL system, which can translate input language to a simplified representation by identifying linguistic patterns such as sentence-specific lexical sets. This simplified representation boosts the overall system's performance by bypassing the domain-specific linguistic patterns during translation. We tested our method using the SPAN-ACT dataset, achieving significant improvements of 8.0% and 8.3% in execution accuracy compared to the system without auxiliary task models, particularly when the systems were trained with and without domain-specific training data respectively. Notably, the new method outperformed current state-of-the-art systems even when it lacked domain-specific training data, showcasing its performance in both scenarios.

This research investigates how to coordinate the movement of multiple robots within the same space, focusing on the planning of conventional robots that can be controlled, and assuming that an adversary may manipulate some of these robots' trajectory plans to disrupt others' paths. To tackle this issue, we first develop a framework in the form of a closed strategic game, where each robot's leader computes an optimal course of action that maximizes its survival chances and takes into consideration the potential control limits imposed by its speed and turnability, along with the limitations imposed by its visibility range. To find these optimal trajectories, each robot's leader uses an iterative process that adjusts its path repeatedly until a certain balance is reached. To make the planning process more manageable, we also develop simplified rules that follow a hierarchical order, first considering the impact of a robot's visibility range on its movement, followed by the potential risks associated with other robots that could potentially be controlled by the adversary. Furthermore, we expand our model to include situations in which an adversary selects a suboptimal strategy, and develops variant models that aim to make the planning process as swift as possible by reducing the number of iterations required, either by simplifying the complex interactions between a robot's movement and the other robots' visibility ranges, or by directly aiming to minimize the risks associated with an adversary's potential control limits. All our models have been successfully tested using simulations in environments that range from simple to complex, and the results show that these models make significantly fewer iterations necessary when compared to

Our research involves examining the dark matter distribution within the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Andromeda 25 (And XXV) through the analysis of the orbital motion of the galaxy's member globular clusters. We utilize two different mass models - one that incorporates both visible matter and dark matter within the galaxy, and a more simplified model that only considers the visible matter and a constant radius of dark matter beyond that point. By comparing the predicted and actual orbital paths of the clusters, we determine the amount and density of And XXV's dark matter. We discover a significant reduction in dark matter density at the centre of the galaxy, with our results suggesting a dense central region transitioning to a sparsely populated state. This dense central area contains approximately 3 million times the density of normal space, with our results implying that And XXV does not have a two-phase structure of dark matter. We also determine that And XXV's dark matter accounts for 75% of its total mass, with its total mass totalling 1.9 billion times the mass of the sun. We also conclude that And XXV's dark matter cannot be explained by the presence of a nearby bright galaxy such as M32 due to the significant difference in their motion patterns as depicted in their velocity profiles.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), grant-free access points (GFAPs) with no scheduling or preallocation allow numerous users to simultaneously transmit data to the terminal, which then employs conventional random access techniques to detect and estimate user-specific sequences. In the context of grant-free massive IoT, designing short, distinguishable, and overlapping sequences for multiple users is a crucial challenge. Noting the inherent flaws in existing orthogonal sequences, this paper proposes non-orthogonal sequences (NOSs) as an alternative solution. These NOSs are generated using a novel, two-stage genetic algorithm, which an accompanying simulator has validated as an effective solution, surpassing the performance of traditional orthogonal and semi-orthogonal sequences in terms of joint channel estimation and data decoding.

We've analyzed and compared the thermodynamic coherence of three approximations for humid air modelling: the sorption parameter model, the water activity model, and the alternative water activity model. The first model employs the Lewis-Ranke-Silny Kovskii equation, incorporating temperature and pressure dependencies of water activity. The second model utilizes the dual incompressibility model and eliminates variables, resulting in the modified Goff-Griffiths-Houck equation, which is only valid at constant temperature. The third model type is the alternative water activity model, derived from combining the first two models and eliminating variables, resulting in a Goff-Griffiths-Houck-Lewis-Ranke-Silny Kovskii equation that operates at constant temperature. Among the three models, only the sorption parameter model exhibits thermodynamic coherence. Conversely, the other two models lack coherence and generate errors when calculated at ambient temperature. Furthermore, applying pressure to the sorption parameter model and water activity model will respectively yield the modified Goff-Griffiths-Houck and Goff-Griffiths equations, both displaying superior performance and coherence. These results form the basis for accurate and reliable humid air modelling.

We define a notion called an outer algebra within a matroid framework, specifically relating to the exterior product matroid with its dual. This concept is characterized by outlining a set of parameters that must be met. By building upon this base concept, we establish more advanced ideas: the full outer algebra corresponding to a given matroid, and its subclass comprising minor-free outer algebras. To illustrate the significance of these structures, we demonstrate various applications across diverse fields, including a proof that shows $U_2(n-2)$ has a minor-free outer algebra parameterized by integers from 1 to n-1, and also explores minor-free matrices within these outer algebras. Additionally, we extend the outer algebra concept to a tuple of matrices rather than a single matrix, and also broaden it to a circuit cover rather than an affine dependent set, resulting in the circuit cover algebra parameterization problem, a question that involves finding the most parameterized matroid given a given number of parameters. This problem is also significant in the context of the matrix rank matrix representation parameterization problem, which is known to have an upper limit and can be reduced to the finding of transversal matrices within the outer algebra structure. Lastly, we define an extension of the matroid structure concept, specifically the outer algebra algebraic matroid, and prove that it has a submodular congruence lattic, and also derive the outline for the matroid structure basis definition in terms of the outer algebra concept

Research into uncertainty estimation for automatic speech recognition (ASR) is significant, but largely overlooked within speaker interaction analysis, especially when considering the monitoring of dialogue states. Since accurate dialogue management depends heavily on ASR output, which is often inaccurate and misleading in turn, addressing uncertainty in ASR outcomes is of the utmost importance. We explore the application of the Word Confusion Networks for uncertainty estimation in ASR, which has shown greater utility in dialogue state monitoring, and also, an additional model that, coupled with a pre-trained confusion network, significantly enhances the accuracy of dialogue state monitoring by producing more precise systems performance. Our approach outperforms a baseline by approximately 7% and 3% in the switchboard and MEMSO datasets respectively.

We demonstrate that:
A flag variety of type A is associated with a smooth Gorenstein Calabi-Yau curve if and only if it is associated with a Deligne-Mumford stack of type A.
Consequently, we identify all flag varieties of type A that are associated with a Deligne-Mumford stack of type A, by combining criteria including a generalised condition of 'no reflected components' and the consideration of exceptional lines.

Lippert, Ponomarenko, and Voigt have developed a novel approach to a broad range of flow problems, including those on discrete structures, in combinatorial geometry, and in set theory. Utilizing only O(n) arithmetic operations, their method can exactly solve discrete flow problems featuring universal algorithms. However, a significant drawback arises when considering space complexity. The researchers's method requires a substantial amount of storage space, potentially exceeding available limits for large datasets on standard computers. As an example, attempting to store the entire result on a single disk file would involve an infeasible number of files, specifically 2^929. To mitigate this limitation, the authors suggest splitting the algorithm into multiple chunks when handling extremely large datasets, but a comprehensive discussion on this adaptation remains unexplored in their research. To address these limitations, the authors should have also explored alternative solutions, such as faster but less accurate approximation algorithms that require less storage space and can be found in the research paper.

Quantum systems exist as complex entities comprising multiple dimensions rather than the singular dimension found in conventional systems. Therefore, accurately determining their quantum properties involves overcoming two significant challenges: distinguishing between different types of quantum correlations present, such as entanglement and classical correlations, and limiting measurement errors. Theoretical frameworks have been developed to address these issues, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to create optimal measurement protocols. Specifically, methods have been established to confirm entanglement in two-qubit systems, including the well-known Schmidt rank approach, and more recent methods for quantifying entanglement in multidimensional systems, which focus on minimizing measurement errors and detecting classical correlations. Although these methods have been extensively studied, their practical application remains underdeveloped, particularly in relation to detecting entanglement in two-qubit systems using optimal measurement protocols. This research builds upon existing theories, deriving a method to assess entanglement in two-qubit systems based on optimal measurements in line with the Schmidt rank framework. The method obtained through this study offers a simpler and more transparent approach than existing approaches for confirming entanglement in two-qubit systems, including the well-known Schmidt rank method, and demonstrates its application through the analysis of a damped two-qubit system.

The characteristics of a distinct palm tree mode (PTM) observed in the JET tokamak magnetohydrodynamic spectrum are examined in detail. A thorough investigation, incorporating discharge data from the JET Enhanced Pulse (E-pulse) campaign in 2009, the M-mode campaign in 2011 and the W-distance campaign in 2009-2019, reveals that PTMs arise from edge ELMs triggered by a specific type of edge turbulence. Analysis of the data indicates that PTMs are evenly distributed across various discharge scenarios and are characterized by a narrow q-profile. While PTMs persist in an quasi-stationary state, they eventually lead to Type-I ELMs. In addition, these researches reveal that PTMs are influenced by the edge magnetic field and are enhanced by an increase in Z boson density. As a result, PTMs may be more difficult to control in scenarios with high fueling levels, narrowing the window for edge stabilization attempts.

This study examines the utilization of pre-trained models in continuous learning and contends that the complexity of resulting methods is unjustified. The main argument posits that the advantage of employing a pre-trained network lies in its ability to capture high-level, across-task patterns, and it therefore seems illogical to expect it to handle low-level, within-task details, particularly when such details can be learned through a simpler approach. To test this idea, the researchers re-evaluate three prominent continual learning methods using four diverse dataset combinations and a straightforward yet effective alternative method that adjusts the final layer alone, and found that a more substantial network layer is not necessary to achieve continuity learning benefits. Additionally, the study investigates the influence of the size of new tasks on the performance of the continual learning methods, and suggests exploring simpler approaches that leverage pre-trained models' high-level representations.

The rapid dissemination of information on social networks poses significant threats, including hate speech that can harm users. Research in this area has primarily focused on incorporating linguistic and non-linguistic features to improve hate speech detection. Our proposed model differs from previous approaches by leveraging a mixture of visible and hidden visual elements in online platforms. Furthermore, our paper outlines current solutions to address the challenges associated with the extraction and integration of social media captions, emojis, and images, as well as the limitation of available labeled data. 😊 Experimental results demonstrate that by relying on a combination of rare and readily available labeled data as well as common and uncommon visual information, our approach significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art solutions in hate speech identification, with an impressive performance of 🎯 96.21% F1-score on Facebook data and 🎯 91.25% F1-score on Twitter data. 📊

This paper investigates the effects of varying degree distributions in large networks of Type-I neurons, focusing on phase angle dynamics. We introduce a metric to evaluate the departure from complete synchronization. For networks with Poisson-distributed connectivities, we derive an analytical equation to predict the transition point to complete synchronization and identify its sensitivity to degree distribution. We also reveal that degree heterogeneity, characterized by the coefficient of variation, strongly influences the non-polarized state existence window, making it broader with increased heterogeneity. Moreover, we find that the non-polarized state can be stabilized even when degree fluctuations become significant. These findings imply that degree distribution plays a crucial role in completing the transition process to complete synchronization in neuronal networks.

The search for an optimal repair in Automated Program Repair (APR) is hindered by an immense solution space, prompting the use of evolutionary computation techniques. This paper examines how conflicting APR approaches can be combined to leverage their unique problem-solving strengths and weaknesses. By integrating two methods, the new method outperforms existing solutions. It's then demonstrated how its fundamental principle of antagonistic cooperation can be applied to other complex software engineering problems.

This article develops a concept called data spectrum, and uses this concept to define the capability region of a generalized inference function as its probability exceeds a certain threshold. The data spectrum is essentially a generalized version of the cumulative sum of a generalized inference function, and it has been shown to be a measure that characterizes complex data sets. The capability region is a set of values that a variable can take, and it has been shown to be related to the data spectrum with a certain threshold. The data spectrum approach is an innovative method that assigns a value to data sets, and it has been shown to be a measure that characterizes complex data sets. The capability region provides a summary of the likelihood of a variable taking certain values, and it has been shown to be a useful tool in understanding the data. The data spectrum approach is an independent method that depends only on the data, and it has been shown to be a measure that is not affected by the underlying distribution. The data spectrum approach is an alternative to traditional statistical methods, and it has been shown to be a simple method that can be used in frequency domain inference.

We introduce a novel method to analyze the flow characteristics of heavy heavy ions by examining their interactions. Through 3-dimensional flow examination, we link the asymmetry in flow patterns to the characteristics of ion collisions, thereby gaining insight into how ions behave under extreme conditions. This method allows us to investigate how fluid dynamics and statistical mechanics apply to such extreme interactions, providing a way to determine the equation-of-state of a single particle beyond its normal stable state. Although this approach is conceptual for now due to the require of 3D data analysis, it offers a unique prospect to gain precise understanding of a single particle's behavior in extreme conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic is still an ongoing global health crisis in second decade despite being first reported in late 2019. Various machine learning-based healthcare applications have been using individual health data to provide personalized services and support contact tracing, medication adherence monitoring, and predicting disease risk among users. Nevertheless, using personal health data for public good at times puts these individuals' confidentiality at risk. While public health security measures are mandatory, we must also consider the confidentiality of the participants in non-mandatory COVID-19 related services. To address this issue, we have developed a technique to safeguard health data confidentiality for non-mandatory COVID-19 related services. Specifically, we have successfully trained a model to spot potential coronavirus patients without putting personal health data confidentiality at risk. Our technique works by adapting a model to withstand attempts to manipulate its input data, thereby safeguarding participant confidentiality. To our knowledge, this method is a pioneering example of using adversarial training to protect privacy in dynamic healthcare environments, particularly in contexts such as coronavirus risk assessment. Our experiments have shown that our technique is effective in identifying early-stage coronavirus patients while protecting participant confidentiality. Furthermore, we have demonstrated its effectiveness in protecting participant confidentiality in even more complex scenarios.

Graph neural networks have shown remarkable capabilities in extracting valuable information from complex data arrangements. This paper explores the potential of GNNs as intelligent processors in wireless communication systems, enabling the extraction of crucial information from diverse wireless signals. With GNNs, the complexity of the processing architecture and the power consumption of the front-end radio can be substantially minimized. A comprehensive analysis and simulation of the performance are conveyed through numerical assessments that demonstrate notable reductions in error rates and power consumption, contingent on the specific wireless application in question.

The trend in a country's crime rates is primarily influenced by specific regional and temporal factors, resulting in noticeable variations in the frequency of crimes across geographic clusters and time periods. This research utilizes a well-known statistical tool, the cluster standard method, to pinpoint distinct regions where crime rates deviate significantly from average, while accounting for potential confounding variables. Employing this analytical framework, this study explores the pattern of changes in a particular type of violent crime, namely, homicide, within the Brazilian state of Goias over a 13-year period (2002-2014). By utilizing data from the Brazilian Ministry of Justice and adjusting for potential biases using spatial regression models, this analysis finds that homicide rates in Goias exhibit significant regional disparities. While the state as a whole experienced an increase in this type of violent crime, with rates rising by about 38.3 percent, certain geographic clusters within the state exhibited more extreme variations, ranging from a 71.0 percent decline in one region to increases exceeding 100 percent in another. This study further analyzes the primary factors contributing to these disparities, revealing that differences in income levels and law enforcement presence play a significant role in shaping the pattern of changes in homicide rates across various geographic regions of Goias.

We focus on accelerating stochastic gradient descent (SGD) while ensuring its validity, yielding results that are grounded in the theory of SGD. Our outcomes are applied to two crucial challenges: maintaining SGD's convergence and protecting it against divergence. Firstly, we investigate a learning rate adjustment formula that accelerates training (achieving an optimal rate) without compromising convergence. Although this issue has received limited attention in the literature, our proposed method is validated through stochastic optimization of least squares regression, both in experiments and the theoretical context, and is also shown to be applicable to optimization of training logistic regression. Secondly, we address the problem of divergence and develop a straightforward approach based on data normalization that eliminates the risk of divergence in SGD, while simultaneously enabling a faster rate of convergence. This method is not only theoretically justifiable but also experimentally verified to be effective.

We propose using a newly designed solar barometer within BabyIAXO to investigate 
the Sun's axion-to-photon transition rate. This innovative tool has the potential 
to either confirm the Standard Solar Model or the $\tau^+$ neutrino oscillation 
hypothesis, known as the LESA effect. By setting two-source parameters based on 
data from solar neutrino experiments and solar oscillations, we establish a 
range for the Sun's axion-to-photon rate. We then explore the feasibility of 
the BabyIAXO experiment to test this condition, keeping in mind that a 
positive result would have significant implications for both the Standard Solar 
Model and the LESA effect.

We have recently discovered that oscillating systems with exceptional resonance, represented by a map, exhibit new types of behavior. Notably, these systems show extended resonance, encompassing large regions, and give rise to complex dynamics, featuring multi-trajectory attractors, leading to intriguing phenomena such as delayed resonance rise, abrupt resonance increases, and intriguing delays in transition. Additionally, we have observed an inverse process where repelling regions initially decrease before suddenly increasing in resonance. This discovery is highly influenced by the characteristics of exceptional resonance, stretching over extensive areas, and follows a simple rule that can be universally applied.

Collecting robotic grasps via simulation has become a highly sought-after goal in robotics, particularly for objects with complex shapes. However, current approaches often rely on traditional methods like random sampling, which can be very slow and apply only partially to certain objects. Additionally, these methods typically require additional support during the grasp collection process, like suction cups, which can be unnecessary and in the way. And so, they end up only half-successful in their mission. Existing tools also often come with a lot of baggage that makes them hard to get a grasp on. And when you do finally collect some grasps, there's a good chance they won't all work, and they won't tell you much about why they didn't. All of this can make robotic grasp collection a real bottleneck. And so, we decided to create a new approach, one that collects as many grasps as possible from a given object with a given shape. We called it DexGraspNet, short for dexterous grasp collection network. And with a little bit of training, it becomes one of the 10 most efficient and effective grasp collectors out there. And the best part? You can use it without any special tools or support. And with a little bit of translation, it becomes one of the most universal grasp collectors out there too. A novel approach to turbo spin echo sequences that minimize effects from respiratory variation has been developed, leveraging advanced modeling and data analysis techniques to create high-resolution images. By employing a multi-phase technique and analyzing signal patterns, the method can accurately reconstruct detailed scans despite the impact of respiratory fluctuation. Comprehensive tests were conducted using diverse scanning areas and a variety of modeling techniques were analyzed to create a high-quality, four-dimensional image set. By comparing our method to a widely-used reference approach over 20 patients, we found that our technique provided better image quality with more accurate reconstruction of lung tissue, the aorta, and the diaphragm. As a result, this advancement offers significant clinical benefits with minimal additional scanning time required.

Model compression through knowledge distillation typically improves computation efficiency, however several studies reveal that the distillation procedure itself incurs significant additional energy expenditures which surpass the savings achieved upon compression. We propose a novel knowledge distillation technique named \emph{InDistill} that seamlessly integrates model compression and acceleration, eliminating the need for a two-stage process. Traditional knowledge distillation forces a smaller model to approximate the entire behavior of a larger model, contrasting our approach where we match only the portions of a model's behavior directly influenced by input data. This results in a notable reduction in the gap between model capacity and data distribution observed in previous studies. We leverage this insight to design a bi-objective knowledge distillation method that minimizes the difference between compressed and original models, as well as matches their responses to input data. This approach yields substantial training speed improvements for tasks involving image and video data.

We define a set-theoretic equivalence $\mathcal{S}$ between two-dimensional manifolds and investigate its properties within the context of smooth functions on the plane that satisfy specific geometric constraints. Specifically, we find that two linear-like functions are $\mathcal{S}$-equivalent if and only if their level sets exhibit a set-theoretic equivalence that is preserved under continuous morphisms. Furthermore, we show that a pair of linear-like functions on the plane have $\mathcal{S}$-equivalent leaf foliations if and only if they themselves are $\mathcal{S}$-equivalent, and this equivalence can be determined via an equivalence that preserves structure presiding over the foliations.

This study investigates the impact of non-resident grazing on the evolution of dry-land vegetation. In this scenario, mobile grazing can survive severe environmental conditions but relies on periodic replenishment of fresh stock due to limitations in withstanding prolonged periods of drought. Our research extends an existing model of dry-land vegetation and grazing interactions by incorporating the grazing's finite capacity and periodic replenishment. We then examine the long-term consequences of this combined system for both the grazing and the vegetation. Our analysis shows that an equilibrium where the grazing consistently depletes and replenishes has a stable dynamic effect on the vegetation population. Additionally, we found that an increase in the grazing's capacity leads to increased oscillations in the vegetation population. We also found that in some situations, the grazing population can experience damped growth, contrasting its typically unstable dynamic behavior when there is consistent activity.

The CountSketch sketch, which is based on linear algebra, efficiently detects dense patterns within large matrices by utilizing a minimal number of storage units. Specifically, it can guarantee that heavy patterns will be detected using at least $d_k/\delta^2$ rows, where $d_k$ represents the largest eigenvalue of a given matrix and $\delta$ is an desired failure rate. 

Our study reveals that we can ensure the presence of heavy patterns within large matrices by introducing specific constraints on these matrices. These rules state that heavy patterns must exist in certain types of matrices with highly variable entries, which are characterized by a linear relationship between the number of rows and columns, as well as a column-to-row ratio that is at least 1. 

These results can be extended to more general types of matrices through the application of eigenvalue perturbation theory. Additionally, we confirm that dense patterns in matrices can be detected using a nearly-optimal number of storage units when these patterns exhibit uniform density across the matrix. 

Lastly, our study highlights the connection between the CountSketch sketch and decision-making tasks, and it establishes a lower bound on the number of storage units required to ensure the presence of heavy patterns within certain types of matrices. This lower bound is closely related to the size of the matrix and the density of the patterns, specifically $\Omega(d_{kk} \log k)$, which implies that we can efficiently design CountSketch-like sketches for dense pattern detection.

A Python-based program, ipie, is introduced for performing auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations and is discussed in its various forms, including its utility in accelerating computational tasks on both central processing units and graphics processing units. ipie offers a high level of flexibility through its modular design which allows for the easy incorporation of multiple, interchangeable propagation schemes. The program includes an intuitive interface for executing simulations on both CPUs and GPUs with a common programming language used throughout, specifically, Python. This program's source code is publicly available and is hosted on GitHub where it can be accessed for free at github.com/trickington/ipie.

A binary decision-making process, the Quantum Prisoner's Conundrum, has been developed as a quantum counterpart to the classic Prisoner's Dilemma game. This process takes advantage of quantum computing principles, enabling players to sample classical outcomes and making decisions based on quantum probabilities. A possible application of the Quantum Prisoner's Conundrum is proposed, involving two financial entities engaging in high-speed trading on a cloud-based platform, which could lead to reduced transaction fees by leveraging quantum computing. To illustrate its relevance, a trading scenario on the Microsoft Quantum Kernel is presented, showing that the Quantum Prisoner's Conundrum could lead to a more profitable outcome for the two entities in terms of reduced fees.

We investigated a market where utility-driven buyers acquire goods from suppliers who adjust their prices based on demand. In the absence of intermediaries, a buyer's demand curve would intersect with the supplier's price function, and we analyzed how the absence of a shared price system affects market outcomes. Our findings reveal that without price standardization, some buyers may receive subpar prices compared to what they would get if prices were known in advance. Our research also showed that price dissemination can always benefit the suppliers, and we introduced various approaches for ensuring optimal worker-wallet assignments in this context.

To facilitate reading comprehension, abstractive summarization must combine a deep understanding of source content with the ability to express ideas in a general knowledge base. Current systems, however, often equate source and target languages without recognizing they contain distinct information. In an attempt to bridge this gap, researchers are exploring entity-centric prompts, commonly used in tasks like question-answering, as a means to acquire general knowledge and facilitate innovative applications. Nonetheless, existing prompt-based methods are generally limited in scope, leading researchers to propose a dynamic approach where specific entity prompts are integrated into a system over time. In this paper, researchers introduce a planning method to automatically adjust entity prompts and thereby expand the scope of acquired knowledge. In experiments involving abstractive summarization, this approach is compared to a method that randomly selects prompts. While the planned method does enhance performance and lead to higher summary quality, the gap in performance remains relatively small. Therefore, in an effort to further improve results, the authors of the entity-centric prompt idea propose a more comprehensive framework that incorporates multiple entity prompts, thereby enabling acquired knowledge to be more extensively integrated.

This research aims to investigate the differentiability of a given n-dimensional function,
which is defined as $F(x) = N\int_{\Omega^{*}}f(x,\xi)\frac{\partial
\zeta^{N}(x)\varphi(\xi)}{\partial x^{j}}d\xi, where $x$ belongs to a domain in n-space and $N$ is a positive integer times a function $f$ evaluated at $x$ and a unit vector $\xi$ in n-space, and a Jordan measure-preserving function $\varphi$ on the unit hyperplane. We establish that if the differentiability of $\varphi$ at a point is known for one dimension less, then the n-dimensional function $F(x)$ is differentiable almost everywhere, with its derivative being expressed as a linear combination of the differentiability of $\varphi$ at that point. Furthermore, under the same conditions, we demonstrate that the n-dimensional function $G(x) = N\int_{\Omega^{*}}\varphi(\xi)a(x, \xi)d\xaif$ is differentiable everywhere and its gradient can be expressed as a linear combination of the differentiability of $\varphi$ at that point.

Research has confirmed that vocal synchronization during face-to-face conversations
enhances communication clarity and comprehension. Achieving successful vocal coordination
in conversations requires adjusting voice tempo in relation to the other speaker's pace.
We have developed an innovative metric and a corresponding method for measuring the level
of vocal coordination displayed in conversations, which focuses on adapting voice speed
in relation to the other speaker's rate. The proposed metric is designed to evaluate vocal
synchronization, and it is different from previous methods that only examine the overall voice
speed) in conversations. Instead, it takes into consideration the context and dynamic nature
of voice tempo adjustments during interactions. The performance of this new metric has been
evaluated through an experiment involving English and Mandarin dialogues recorded in controlled
settings, and also using video conferencing software. The results show that vocal coordination
occurs spontaneously and efficiently in conversations, even without prior knowledge or
experience. The developed method is also capable of identifying individuals with difficulties
with vocal coordination.

Recent research in control theory for an arbitrary qubit state, represented as a point on the unitary sphere, discovered a Lagrange symmetric manifold called Lambda-S1. This led to the development of two generalized versions of the Heisenberg-Purcell evolution operator, as well as a fundamental categorical model of qubit manipulation. The proposed framework in this letter provides a novel approach for describing quantum systems, regardless of their complexity, using arbitrary unitary transformations. The model is further reinforced by demonstrating that the categorical model of qubit motion is equivalent to free motion in the group U(2). Using a suitable coordinate system, we have derived a explicit formula for the evolution operator, as proven by Zalba et al. Our work, however, reveals that this equation corresponds to the hyperboloid equation within the Lagrange symmetric manifold Lambda-S1. The proposed operator allows for efficient manipulation of qubit states, and our experiments confirm that it achieves the shortest possible length for implementing CP maps within the convex hull of rotations.

Analytical calculations have been conducted for two types of quasiparticle excitations
in the fractional quantum Hall effect, specifically for the charge and neutral flux quasiparticles.
In the energy spectrum of charge quasiparticle configurations, exact analytical solutions
have been derived for up to 30 trial states of the effective magnetic field, providing precise convergence.
The calculations yield the exact values at 4 specific points, giving rise to critical energies.
The critical energies display a singularity in their derivatives and their ratios follow a specific sequence.
On the other hand, analytical expressions for the neutral flux quasiparticle configurations have been obtained
for an infinite number of states, up to an infinite number of terms, providing highly accurate convergence.
The findings obtained can serve as benchmarks for numerical methods and may facilitate the evaluation of critical energies through perturbation theory, given their complex nature.

In the context of rheology, polycrystalline ice's evolution is modeled using the compressive-plasticity Stokes variational inequality. Specifically, this model applies to West Antarctic ice sheets where pure creep ice is surrounded by clasts. We focus on the dynamic variational inequality which governs quasi-static processes, and we investigate numerical solutions' convergence for a simplified 2D version of this problem. We demonstrate that by employing the finite element method with sufficient spatial and temporal discretization, we can obtain consistent and stable approximations.

Galactic bursts occur when a disk galaxy experiences a rapid increase in star formation. This intense star-forming activity is typically accompanied by a rapid increase in superglobal outflows. However, it is unclear what controls the outflows and their impact on the outflows' shape and outflow velocity. Using observations from KCWI of the galaxy Pox 68 at the peak of a starburst at a redshift of 0.173, we studied a phenomenon known as feedback regulation. We obtained high-resolution spectra of Pox 68's ionized gas at various positions across its disk of thickness 1.73 arcminutes, which allowed us to map its ionized gas. The distribution of its ionized gas corresponds to a thick disk of thickness 1.73 arcminutes, which is also observed in its companion galaxies Pox69 and Pox70 and is also observed to be tilted relative to the major axis of Pox68 to the extent of approximately 45 degrees. The distribution of its ionized gas also appears to be oriented at an angle of approximately 45 degrees relative to the major axis of Pox68 to the extent of approximately 45 degrees. In this study, researchers examined triangular flow ($v_3$) in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions using a multiphase transport model. They found that, unlike the dipole collectivity, the quadrupole $v_3$ showed significant correlations with the initial $v_3$ and centrality, largely due to parton scattering. Investigating both range of scattering probabilities and string-mesh EoS, they discovered that, similar to dipole $v_2$, the quadrupole $v_3$ could also be mainly formed by parton scattering within the medium. Furthermore, using $v_3$ and its correlations with other properties, such as the average transverse momentum and participant number, they found that, similar to $v_2$, the quadrupole $v_3$ showed relatively minimal dependence on the range of scattering probabilities and the fluid-dynamic to scattering cross-section ratio at both energies.

This study examines a novel concept called simultaneous robotic structure (a quantity of robotic bodies working in tandem to create a point of equilibrium). These robots are defended against external assaults, resulting in an area of safety characterized by the term "simultaneous robotic structure" in this context. A condition for determining the exact size of this stability area in n-dimensional space is developed and mathematically formulated. Moreover, a relevant algorithm is presented along with a demonstration using a specific scenario - a robotic sphere array - in the context of a 3D environment where it successfully defends against external assault from a group of opposing entities.

We investigate whether depth estimation, specifically in challenging monocular depth estimation, serves as an improved pre-training task over traditional image classification for semantic segmentation, despite depth estimation seemingly less relevant to semantic segmentation. Surprisingly, our research finds the opposite truth without adjustments, where classification results yield a higher semantic segmentation accuracy. Nevertheless, refining our approach by incorporating two key innovations leads to depth estimation surpassing classification: (a) aligning the monocular depth estimation and semantic segmentation datasets via domain adaptation, and (b) optimizing flow-based depth estimation methods to conform to semantic segmentation targets. The resulting architecture, named Align-DSE, significantly enhances the effectiveness of unsupervised pre-training for semantic segmentation, achieving a 6.1 percentage point gain over classification in val-40 Cityscapes at the exact same number of iterations. Moreover, our architecture is versatile and compatible with a wide range of deep learning models. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/aidg/Align-DSE.

This article aims to find the maximal distortion under a specific constraint for certain types of mappings. Specifically, it focuses on transformations from the unit disk to itself where the constraint involves harmonic logarithmic functions and initial terms in a power series. By imposing additional restrictions on coefficient behavior, we derive maximum distortion limits that surpass existing limits for certain types of mappings. Furthermore, we prove that these derived limits are the highest achievable under these specific conditions.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method to estimate its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces the computational time needed to process large datasets. The simplified method leverages a specific pattern in the data that allows for a more direct calculation of the correlation coefficient. The new method's performance is compared to a standard alternative approach and demonstrates comparable accuracy but with much faster processing speed. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulations that show it preserves the original results while offering substantial improvements in computational efficiency.

To address various challenges in the transportation system, such as traffic management, road conditions, and safety, Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) has emerged as a promising solution. However, in this research, we delve into a more pressing issue: safeguarding private user data within VEC. To achieve this, we propose a comprehensive framework that combines edge computing and edge AI techniques to enhance data privacy. By integrating these concepts, we demonstrate that both efficient computing and intelligent analytics can be achieved while maintaining the privacy of users' sensitive data. Our framework's effectiveness is validated through theoretical analysis and simulation, which shows that it can maintain data privacy to a certain extent, measured by the entropy of remote storage and confirmed by our experimental findings.

We introduce a new subcategory of Euler topology surfaces, which includes the manifold-like surfaces first described by T. Banach in 1998. To define this class, we apply techniques from combinatorial analysis, mapping theory, and surface reconstruction. A key characterization of the Euler topology surfaces is established and various examples of non-manifold-like surfaces providing a complete characterization of the new class are presented. This is followed by an investigation of the surface's 2-dimensional simplicial complex and the construction of the dual graph of the surface, leading to a semi-combinatorial model. Lastly, the surface's reconstruction from its dual graph is established and an algorithm for determining its combinatorial class is derived.

Our predator-prey model builds on the Holling-Tanner framework, taking into account how population density affects prey quality and results in a complex dynamical system. We examine how these dynamics are affected by parameters such as carrying capacity, prey quality adjustment, and predator experience, leading to a system where solutions can exhibit multiple equilibrium points, stable and unstable orbits, and result in the complexification of a previously simple model. We utilize numerical software to analyze these phase portraits, employing parameter values to represent real-world ecosystems where such models apply.

This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the initial phase of the Aspect Pivot Simplex algorithm, a variant of the simplex algorithm for linear programming. The analysis confirms a linear iteration bound under certain general conditions, thereby refining previous time complexity insights. The study also highlights the algorithm's inherent linear iteration deep inside the algorithm with a detailed proof, which sheds light on its underlying mechanism. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated through a deep interior point technique, and its inner loop linear iteration depth is shown to be a distinctive feature distinguishing it from other algorithms. The findings have significant practical implications, indicating that the algorithm will complete both the first and subsequent phases within a linear number of iterations, and this prediction has important theoretical and practical significance for just-in-time algorithms.

This study aims to investigate another modular group, NK\_{1}, alongside Bak's modular group \hat{\mathbb Z}\times\delta, where \delta represents the Coxeter group $(2,\infty,\infty)$ relabeling. We will define NK\_{1} as the graded ring generated by the NK\_{1}-modular classes over \delta, and then establish that NK\_{1} is isomorphic to Bak's modular group \hat{\mathbb Z}\times\delta, where the isomorphism is defined using a map called map-mu. Furthermore, this study will demonstrate that the map-mu sends graded NK\_{1}-subgroups to graded \delta-subgroups, reveal that map-mu is an arithmetic order-preserving map, explore properties of elements within map-mu, identify which elements within map-mu have inverse counterparts within map-mu, and finally, conclude this study by answering whether map-mu is a group-homomorphism.

This paper examines the off-shell and IR-divergent effects on top quark mass reconstruction in ttj events. The study utilizes a multi-stage matching scheme between parton shower and matrix elements that accounts for the influences of both virtual and real radiation corrections. The findings show that neglecting off-shell and IR-divergent contributions results in substantial systematic uncertainties of 2-4 GeV, albeit with an underlying trend, in agreement with previous research. Moreover, an alternative method for addressing these corrections that modulates the shape of pT,tt has been reassessed. The extraction of the top quark pole mass from simulated data with an integrated luminosity of 300 fb^-1 yields a mean value of 172.25 GeV with a 3.3 GeV standard deviation, consistent with the world average.

Recent advancements in template-free facial recognition systems have shown their potential, incorporating self-attention mechanisms in their architecture. The highest overall performance to date has been achieved by a vision transformer (vIT), utilizing the CIFAR-10 dataset. However, the vIT model is computationally expensive and requires a significant amount of data to effectively learn facial features. In this research, we assess the vIT model's effectiveness when used for zero-shot facial identification and counterfeiting, applying various datasets to evaluate its performance. Additionally, we investigate the model's sensitivity to hyperparameter adjustments and data availability.

Recent advancements in Deep Reinforcement Learning have led to significant progress in automated vehicles. Despite this progress, most models have been evaluated in simulated environments, with some failing to adapt to real-world settings.
