This conclusion is still applicable even when considering subsequent research improving the security analysis of RSOPe.

This research paper confirms that certain curve properties are unique among
timelike Bertrand curves in pseudo-Riemannian spaces. Specifically, we've
demographically verified that only geodesic curves meet the criteria for
Bertrand curves of order two within a pseudo-Riemannian space. Additionally,
we've found that non-geodesic Bertrand curves of order two cannot exist in
Riemannian spaces. Further analysis reveals that Bertrand curves of any order
exhibit constant torsion if and only if they are straight lines.

We investigate the potential for Feller diffusion combinations to serve as models of real-world nonliving systems. To build these combinations, we develop an approach involving the use of linearly linked combinations of diffusion processes. Furthermore, by applying probabilistic principles, we establish sufficient conditions for the resulting combinations, which are represented as Feller diffusion matrices, to possess collectivity, non-negativity and smoothness properties. Ultimately, this work provides a framework for calculating the characteristic functions of diffusion models through the application of a transformation of variables along with a transfer operator based on an initial stochastic model.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems that facilitate non-resonant scattering operations. These methods allow us to investigate multi-photon scattering processes within both linear and nonlinear waveguide QED systems by considering interacting photons and auxiliary systems. By applying the wave function matching method, we have developed a fully diagrammatic approach to calculate the \(S\) matrix in waveguide QED systems. This approach applies to both single and multi-photon scattering processes. By applying the rotating wave approximation, we have derived a set of rules for diagrammatic calculations in waveguide QED systems. These rules are capable of describing all single photon scattering processes. However, when non-conserving interactions are involved, we have developed an additional set of rules that can describe scattering processes even in the absence of rotating wave approximation. This has allowed us to explore diagrammatic methods in non-resonant scattering operations even in systems with complex and non-traditional interactions. By applying these methods, we have calculated the \(S\) matrix in both linear and nonlinear two and three level systems. These calculations have yielded results that align with other methods in waveguide QED systems. This has validated the accuracy and feasibility of diagrammatic methods in describing scattering processes within waveguide QED systems. This approach applies to both single and multi-photon scattering processes. However, when dealing with non-conserving interactions, we have realized that the long range principle must be applied cautiously in waveguide QED systems.

A boosted dark energy model incorporating spin-dependent particle number is
examined in its diffused form across space. Initially, the cosmological equation
of state for this model is determined analytically, and subsequently, numerical
simulations are used to investigate the spin-dependent feature in greater
detail. These studies enable a deeper comprehension of the black hole decay
mechanism described by the CPT-boosted dark energy theory (BDET). In analyses
of the baryon asymmetry, our findings suggest that a very small percentage
of BDE consists of left-handed antiparticles. Moreover, a spin-dependent
diffusion coefficient is defined and inserted into the equation set. Following
numerical solution, our results pinpoint the phase where the dark energy
measures its spin, resulting in a spin-dependent feature being established in BDE
and subsequently transferred throughout the universe. Additionally, a
correspondence is made between the model's behavior and that of the
CPT-boosted dark energy theory (BDET). Lastly, our studies' implications and
potential applications are explored, and a possible connection between the
model and a particle physics candidate known as the baryon asymmetry-related axio-
higgsino particle (bahip) is investigated.

This note proves two famous identities, known as the Bauer-Assous-Diaz identity and the generalized Faulhaber and Euler constants, through the use of modular forms and the reexpression of the theta constant in terms of a Fourier series.

This research examines an unconventional method for improving traditional
differential continuous phase modulation detection techniques by incorporating
fixed-length delays into received signals, s(t), to create s'(t). The proposed
detection method relies on its ability to represent traditional differential
continuous phase modulation detection, which operates without explicit phase
encoding. Analytical expressions for the bit error rate (BER) of signals with
various modulation formats, including aligned and aligned-non-aligned cases,
are derived. Comparative analysis with standard differential detection reveals that
introducing a 2N-symbol delay can boost signal-to-noise ratio by at least 3dB
for popular continuous phase modulation formats, including aligned-binary and
aligned-4PAM, while maintaining BER performance equivalence.

A major shortcoming of traditional reward learning algorithms is that they consume excessive time due to repetitive and costly trial and error processes, necessitating lengthy and complicated setup for data collection. This paper presents an efficient reward function learning method utilizing observed video data and temporal ranking information to significantly reduce data collection time. Initially, the video footages are organized into temporal clusters based on the transition frequencies, employing the VideoMTS ranking algorithm. This algorithm co-opts the video editor's intuition to identify essential movement characteristics. Next, the ranked video segments are utilized to develop a compact transition-based reward function. Notably, this function alone can facilitate notable navigation skills for diverse environments, even when primarily based on basic keyboard inputs. However, to enhance the learned skill's robustness and efficiency across a broader spectrum of tasks and situations, we propose two additional techniques: the integration of multiple video clusters and the use of video segments featuring visually appealing movements, both of which involve adjusting the transition-based reward function. Experimental results on multiple platforms and datasets, including FourRoom and other Envirobots, as well as YouTube Hand Movements, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in developing robust and transferable skills with reduced data collection time.

On the light front, nucleons are described using a specific type of field theory within a noncommutative space-time framework. In this theory, nucleons are constructed using quarks and gluons, which obey light-cone gauge for both the proton and the neutron. Newly introduced functions, known as nucleon configuration functions, are used to describe the distribution of quarks and gluons within the nucleons, which adhere to specific relations among themselves and with the nucleon wave functions. These functions, when used in a specific context, reveal the nucleon structure in line with the principle of quantum mechanics, allowing us to understand the nucleon in different scenarios, whether it's considering the presence of a large noncommutative parameter, an intense magnetic field, or even the interaction between nucleons.

In this context, we examine two variants of the Toric code, incorporating external magnetic fields with a solenoidal character, which encompass both linear and circular patterns. These models are both positioned on a two-dimensional lattice and possess edge configurations that exhibit topological properties, accommodating a variable amount of quantum information, rather than a fixed amount, as seen in the extended Toric code. This research expands and contrasts the analytical and numerical findings from the previously mentioned models with a previously unsolved model incorporating a uniform magnetic field, the rigid Dirac string phase, and a previously proposed model with a variable string length, the elastic string phase. This research delves into the quantitative and qualitative distinctions of these phases, including their impact on entanglement entropy, a measure that topological order typically resists degradation from local disturbances, and explores phase transitions and relationships between these phases, supported by extensive numerical simulations that confirm theoretical predictions, demonstrating the robustness and distinct characteristics of these models in their phase transitions.

We investigate in-depth the properties of complex, Hermitian random band matrices subjected to specific low-rank transformations. These transformations lead to intricate behavior in the associated eigenvalue distributions, as evidenced by the emergence of singularities within the associated non-Hermitian eigenvalue density, affecting specific intervals depending on the model parameters. Leveraging a non-Hermitian eigenfunction representation, we apply the method of sigma-model approximation to analyze the behavior of these transformed models. This approach enables us to derive power-law scaling behaviors for eigenvalue distributions in the vicinity of these singularities. Notably, our results affirm the existence of typical typical eigenfunctions for these transformed models.

Recent advancements in conversational AI models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a wide variety of tasks. The method generally entails fine-tuning on a large dataset of unlabelled dialogue text paired with the corresponding conversation context. The approach has shown positive results, but it is worth noting that this context is often irrelevant to the dialogue content, which may lead to the incorporation of less meaningful components during the pre-training phase. This research aims to address this limitation by introducing a meaningfulness filter to guide pre-training. The filter leverages the cosine similarity between the dialogue history and a lexical database to assess the significance of dialogue content. By establishing a threshold for this similarity, only meaningful segments are retained for training. To achieve this, we re-designed the pre-training objectives to exclude irrelevant dialogue segments. Our proposed approach, dubbed Meaningful Pre-training for Conversation Comprehension (MPCC), is evaluated on StackExchange, WikiTalk, and Switchboard datasets, yielding improved performance at various levels of significance thresholds.

As deep learning models increase in complexity, their ability to be understood and explain their decisions remains limited. Despite this, there's no universally accepted standard for measuring the interpretability of machine learning algorithms.

We propose a new framework for assessing interpretability, one that's tailored to how humans learn and understand these models. By examining three essential modules - data input, algorithmic process, and explanation provided - we analyze and refine the concept of interpretability.

Through this framework, we identify three fundamental cognitive processes: 1) recognizing the algorithm's input and output criteria, 2) comprehending how the algorithm operates, and 3) getting clear explanations from the model.

We use a novel metric - Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS) - to quantify the complexity of each module, providing a quantitative measure to evaluate a algorithm's ease of interpretation.

We tested our framework with six popular data-mining algorithms, evaluating their interpretability using both human learning and the CIS method. The results showed that some algorithms, like Decision Trees and KNN, are relatively easy to understand, while others, such as Random Forest and Neural Networks, are more challenging for humans to comprehend.

We believe that by developing a shared understanding of the concept of interpretability, we can bridge the gap between machine learning and human learning, making models that are easier to learn from and trust.

Anomaly detection without supervision is a complicated task. In the context of the Whistler Online Anomaly Detection Workshop, multiple one-shot anomaly detection algorithms were presented, some relying on projection-based methods, others using deep learning, and a few with generalized approaches. However, only a few offered the compactness and adaptability required to support the development of efficient, self-contained anomaly detectors. In response to this challenge, we created TiWS-iForest, a version of the widely used isolation tree algorithm, tailored for the events where computational resources are limited and only a single sample is available for support. Furthermore, we conducted a series of experiments that not only evaluated the performance of the proposed method, as compared to existing one-shot anomaly detection algorithms, but also explored its compatibility with a recently proposed unsupervised anomaly detection technique focused on small ML models.

A novel approach that translates non-stationary extreme value data into stationary data is explored, utilizing a Poisson process representation. This technique's Bayesian inference for the parameters in the resulting standard extreme value process is more efficient from a computational perspective because it doesn't involve sampling extreme values. Instead, a formula expressing total excesses over high thresholds uses a a two-dimensional Poisson process, which is partitioned into a standard extreme value process and a "noise" process. The parameters in the standard extreme value process are then estimated by relating their values in a two-dimensional parameterization to those in a one-dimensional parameterization. This allows for a method similar to parameterization reparameterization, which involves updating the prior distribution for one parameter based on the current values of the other parameters. This new approach is demonstrated on simulated data from a standard extreme value distribution and through comparison of a scale parameter estimates from a method in the literature and a method that takes into account information from a larger portion of the parameter space. Finally, the reparameterization method is utilized in a case study of extreme sea levels at locations in the UK.

We examine the properties of a cross section in the context of a specific process, and seek to identify areas on a parameter space where this cross section attains its stationary points. To accomplish this, we employ a differential cross section model based on the Bumpiness model of Barten. By constructing a corresponding Legendre-Fenchel transform, we are able to determine a polyhedral region in which the cross section exhibits stationary points. Additionally, we develop a geometric method for identifying and characterizing these areas in relation to specific economic indicators.

This research presents an updated version of the COMET-ATOMIC dataset, a comprehensive collection of causal knowledge extracts from ATOMIC, a large dataset of textual descriptions of common-sense causal events. The dataset is curated to enhance the clarity of its causal intentions, making it suitable for advanced representation learning by both symbolic and neural models. Unlike standard machine learning data, the COMET-ATOMIC dataset is designed to capture nuanced causal knowledge by detailing precursor conditions through to their effects, utilizing fine-grained labels and hierarchical structures. To facilitate the development of both symbolic and neural knowledge representation systems, the research proposes a series of challenging tasks centered on COMET-ATOMIC. In these tasks, models must not only identify the dataset's components but also generalize to previously unseen knowledge. Our findings indicate that both traditional symbolic models and cutting-edge neural network architectures are capable of processing the complexity of the COMET-ATOMIC dataset, with neural models ultimately achieving better generalization performance. The research makes available COMET-ATOMIC, along with accompanying benchmarks, code, and model releases to support the development of more advanced and generalizable causal knowledge representation systems.

To determine the properties of dense evolutionary stages of protostellar cores and early protostellar objects within the the Hi-GAL survey's coverage of the Galactic centre within the l = 30 to 50 region, a comprehensive pipeline of data analysis was developed and implemented. This critical work requires determining the radii of dust emission peaks outwards from the solar system's boundaries and is based on the use of integrated spectral energy distributions (SEDs) in the sub-millimetre waveband. The implementation involved the use of a Monte Carlo simulation of uncertainty in the data using the XID+ algorithm, a new method for determining peak radii with uniform and accurate results that matches existing scientific findings. The application of this pipeline to the survey's data reveals 349 protostellar objects, consisting of both prestellar objects and those in the densest stages of star formation. These objects include those classified as IY and IIY, representing uncorrected and corrected data through dust colour temperature correction, and totalising 349 and 353 objects respectively. This data includes 102 objects of class CV, CVY, and IIY, primarily influencing the IIY class and revealing 353 objects including those in the filament of CGPS J035.68+6112. This significantly larger count than expected highlights the difficulty and need for accurate data interpretation in this region. Furthermore, data analysis also revealed 134 CV and IIY protostellar objects, revealing initial and final mass ranges from 0

The study of old, metal-poor stars in globular clusters like NGC 2808 offers crucial insights into the early universe, making it an important subject of research. These stars are thought to have formed shortly after the Big Bang, and their composition is a window into the earliest periods of cosmic history. A specific cluster, NGC 2808, is notable for its homogeneous appearance but may, in fact, be composed of multiple sub-populations. In the absence of detailed abundance data, this possibility had been largely speculative. However, a recent investigation using MUSE and HIRES data has made it possible to accurately determine the abundances of several initial population stars in the cluster. Notably, these new measurements confirm a variation in metallicity, a trend that is seen when considering [α/Fe] across the different samples. A second set of data collected for some of these initial population stars using HIRES has further validated the earlier results, and together, they provide substantial evidence that NGC 2808 contains two distinct, metal-rich populations with higher α-abundance. These new findings have significant implications for the study of multiple population clusters, and in particular, they highlight the need to exercise caution when assuming homogeneity in the determination of cluster parameters.

For initial exit events from a one-dimensional corridor in a filamentous model, we have derived the mean and variance of duration until exit, expressed in terms of time and position of the first exit location. Additionally, we have established a formula for the initial exit probability in a semi-infinite domain as a function of time and the position of the exit location. These results, which were obtained through asymptotic analysis and considering the semi-filament limit, demonstrate a strong influence of the confining potential on this probability, resembling an Arrhenius law. Conversely, for the case of a reflecting barrier, we have obtained different mean and variance expressions, which can be expanded into asymptotic series, showing dependence on complex combinations of Bessel and Fresnel functions.

Quantum physics challenges traditional notions of reality, reality's manifestations, and causality, resulting in intriguing yet often perplexing phenomena. Despite this fundamental shift, inductive reasoning in quantum physics often resembles classical approaches, leading to paradoxes like Elitzur-Vaidman's photon polarization measurement. To resolve such discrepancies between quantum predictions and classical reasoning, this study introduces a quantized version of Bayes' theorem. The proposed theorem is then applied to reframe the Elitzur-Vaidman scenario as a genuine case of quantum inference.

In this work, we have developed a novel application of the QCD equation of state, specifically for tiny systems. By combining experimental data from heavy-ion collisions with theoretical models from the QCD equation of state, we have derived crucial information about the system's critical parameters, including its critical temperature and curvature of the critical line. Furthermore, our analysis has provided insight into the value of the speed of sound at the critical point, yielding results that are consistent across different energy scans and theoretical models. These findings support the notion that high-energy collisions with a limited number of particles are an effective means of accessing a critical point in the QCD phase diagram.

The Steenrod Algebra has cohomology groups that are generated by elementary cohomology classes, but this fact doesn't necessarily imply all cohomology generators are elementary, as there could be additional non-ignorable generators that need to be accounted for. However, all such non-ignorable generators can be expressed in terms of elementary cohomology classes, as demonstrated through the use of a specific quadratic operation related to the Steenrod Algebra. It's been discovered that some double Steenrod products exhibit properties similar to commutative derivatives, which has significant implications for simplifying complex calculations in Steenrod Algebra cohomology.

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet optical sets from space are usually contaminated by Lyman-alpha interposing galaxies, resulting in distorted light measurements. Although various techniques such as removal, correction, and cancellation are used to mitigate contamination, they all result in inaccurate white noise levels and systematics. In contrast, employing Lyman-alpha filter models enables maintaining the pure noise characteristics and systematics of ultraviolet photometry by deconvolving the distortion caused by Ly-alpha galaxies and retaining the distortion in the data. As a result, this approach recovers its full sensitivity and sensitivity resolution in applications such as space-based ultraviolet imaging spectroscopy and photometry.

This research explores a distributed control strategy for graph-related networks to address coordination problems, focusing on designing a collective control mechanism using ideal references filtered through graph filters to balance node states at equilibrium points. A stable, automatic feedback control system is achieved by combining a consensus-based control structure with an adaptive gain that depends on the graph Laplacian, leading to a stable output that closely resembles the filtered reference signal up to a distortion factor closely related to the graph's connectivity coalescence speed. Numerical simulations demonstrate the proposed approach's efficacy in various scenario contexts.

This paper outlines a novel technique for automatically indexing and localizing visual content in long-form video recordings, divided into equal segments based on temporal duration. By utilizing convolutional neural networks with shared weight convolutional layers, where each layer's parameters are sequentially adjusted to accommodate varying temporal scales, our method enhances feature extraction at broader scales. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through comparative evaluations on benchmark datasets, which show that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods for action recognition in video sequences. Furthermore, we illustrate the diversity of indexed features at successive scales using dynamic graph visualization.

This study confirms that an unverified transmission model, where the transmitter isn't aware of the receiver's estimation errors, can still result in unconditional security for a specific type of transmission – binary transmission over a noisy channel. Specifically, we derive the exact range of errors within which secure communication remains possible, and our findings demonstrate that secure communication remains feasible up to a certain level of error corresponding to half the channel's bandwidth. Furthermore, we identify the ideal error interval, which corresponds to a unique channel input distribution. These findings also illustrate that in practical applications, secure communication is possible even when errors exceed this ideal range, albeit at a lower rate than the maximum achievable rate.

We investigate the movement of particles within a specific type of energy profile known as washboard potentials, characterized by evenly spaced peaks of varying heights. The particles' transitions between adjacent peaks are of particular interest. Previous studies have examined the movement of particles within this energy profile under certain assumptions, but our research aims to expand on these findings by making fewer assumptions and thus obtaining more general results. The study provides a detailed analysis of the conditions under which particles can move freely between adjacent peaks along the wavy surface, focusing on the critical threshold of energy required for this movement to occur. The study also describes the different phases of physical behavior and demonstrates that even with these more relaxed assumptions, the underlying mathematical approach to the problem remains universal.

Time-of-arrival based localization, a technique used in beyond-Cell identification and localization, relies on exceeding mmWave venue penetration limitations by utilizing immense bandwidths to facilitate high-resolution signals and angle-of-arrival estimation. However, in reality, signal duration is constrained and can be comparable to the time it takes for the signal to travel to a reflector, making the application of conventional localization methods impractical. This paper discusses an advanced method based on an adaptable local projection, where a unified unit vector and angle are derived from the signal's post-processing outputs via an optimization process rather than individual unit vector angle optimizations. The proposed method not only reduces computational complexity but also provides the optimal joint angle and unit vector representation, ultimately resulting in increased precision. Furthermore, this paper discusses the impact of channel models on beyond-Cell identification and localization, highlighting the need to develop advanced channel models to accurately simulate these processes.

We start by using the Heisenberg algebra to develop a quantum representation of the Euclidean group e3 in a way that relates to the Landau quantization of a charge, focusing specifically on its angular momentum. This approach involves encoding the charge's quantum states in a 2D Euclidean space and representing the e3 algebra in this space. As a result, we find that the Landau charge's angular momentum is inherently undefined, highlighting an interesting aspect of the e3 quantum representation. This outcome stems from a non-trivial cohomology in the e3 quantum vector fields, leading to the existence of a non-conserved, self-induced force. This unusual situation resolves a long-standing paradox related to the absence of angular momentum in the Landau quantized charge. Additionally, we explore the relevance of our findings to other physical systems, particularly to the 2D Klein-Gordon equation.

In order to accomplish this task, a hierarchical ontology-based dataset is first constructed. Following a comprehensive exploration of multiple dataset sources, a new "folio" dataset is created that incorporates a significant amount of real-world information. However, due to the limitations of current technology, a purely data-driven approach to recognizing named entities from large sources is not feasible. Therefore, a novel method for recognizing named entities using a combination of hyperbolic neural networks and a hierarchical ontology is developed to overcome this limitation. This method utilizes a multi-layered neural network to first generate low-quality predictions, which are then refined in successive layers until a final accurate outcome is reached. By using a hierarchical ontology to establish connections between the final outcomes of each layer, the method is able to recognize entity categories at various levels of specificity. Experiments conducted on a large folio reveal a significant improvement in entity classification performance within a sequential framework, particularly when compared to traditional non-segmented approaches.

We derive explicit expressions for the Hankel determinants of order two for functions belonging to the general classes $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{S}, representing special types of starlike and strongly starlike functions, in terms of the coefficients of a power series expansion of the function $f(z)$. We utilize a recurrence relation and formula for the Chebyshev polynomials to simplify the determination of the Hankel determinants and provide bounds for the Hankel determinants of order two, as well as the Janowski coefficients for the class $\mathcal{U}$.

In cloud computing environments, users can reserve virtual machines (VMs) in advance to guarantee immediate deployment upon request. Consequently, there are usually a significant number of reserved VMs in data centers before they are actually needed, which poses a problem as these VMs consume valuable physical resources without contributing to revenue generation. To mitigate this issue, our solution – called Prepartition – aims to minimize the number of reserved VMs in a manner acceptable to users, by dynamically adjusting the configuration of VMs and their schedules in data centers. By transforming the problem into a combinatorial optimization issue, our approach relies on a tailored algorithm to effectively solve it, especially during periods of unpredictable user behavior. Experimental results validate the superiority of Prepartition over current solutions.

In the realm of Reinforcement Learning applied to Dynamic Game theory, the lack of general training methods is partly attributed to the instability typically encountered when using conventional policy gradient methods on the manifold of Nash equilibria. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that fixes the action profiles generated by the policy and employs Fixed Point Networks, a variant of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, to approximate the Nash equilibrium equilibrium. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method based on Policy Mirror Descent, minimizing both the fixed point error and the cumulative time-to-equilibrium. This approach has been successfully validated on two intricate multi-agent scenarios: a non-trivial alliance against a common adversary and a stable game with temporary benefits.

In cases where we can't assume that treating a variable affects other variables, we develop a new method to calculate the maximum possible effect of a variable on an outcome variable Y from unobserved scenarios. This new tool, called the total causal effect bound, utilizes polynomials to describe how variables relate to each other, even when their interactions aren't linear. Focusing on specific cases, we show that treating high-dimensional X to yield Y doesn't have a significant causal effect, but we also prove that there are scenarios in which narrowing the search for an optimal strategy for Y by changing some of X results in a substantial improvement, all while ensuring that X and Y have meaningful values in unobserved scenarios as well. This theory is applied to a new algorithm that uses feedback to achieve optimal efficiency in a specific type of problem, called the linear bandit problem. Despite the dimensionality of X being much larger than a polynomial factor, we show that this method converges to the optimal value from unobserved scenarios, making it the first such algorithm to do so without assuming linear correlation between X and Y. This theory is also used to derive more precise estimates for how treating X to yield Y would look in a specific type of model, called the linear structural equation model, under the assumption that X and Y are normally distributed.

This research focuses on enhancing the surveillance capabilities of an LTI system's network to detect and counter stealthy, masquerading attacks more effectively. Previous studies found it challenging to implement this system due to the inherent indistinguishability of normal operation and attack states under a stealthy assault, utilizing small amounts of malicious data. To overcome this issue, we developed an effective model-based detect-theory approach that leverages an LTI system's known characteristics to detect attacks. Our innovative method divides the detection process into two steps: first using data up to a certain point in time known as the "sliding-window period" to identify suspicious patterns using Bayesian statistics, and then using subsequent data to achieve an accurate diagnosis through Bayesian updating. Our analysis shows that the proposed method can successfully reduce the detection resources required compared to other approaches, and is capable of achieving nearly optimal performance with the available data. Our results demonstrate the superiority of this method over other approaches in various scenarios, and show that it can adapt to different attack types and detect them with a set level of confidence. Moreover, the proposed method is scalable and capable of handling complex systems, and its effectiveness in real-world settings can be verified through testing and simulation.

A language interpreter enables translation of spoken words into a different language, whereas a summary is a concise representation of lengthy text, typically generated from a more extensive work. Summaries can either be produced manually or through automated methods, with the latter often relying on sophisticated machine-based techniques to emulate human creativity. Notably, researchers have concentrated more on developing English language summaries utilizing causal transformer models, attention-based models, and similar techniques. However, there is a lack of accessible tools for producing summaries in lesser spoken languages, specifically those where text is written in Indian scripts such as Devanagari, Kannada, and Tamil. In response, we introduce a graphical model-based system to overcome this deficiency. Our proposed system is a general solution that allows it to outperform existing summation tools when assessed using popular metrics. Furthermore, we leverage tools for pre-processing and show the effectiveness of our method through case studies involving summarization in languages that employ these scripts.

We propose the concept of S-rings of Noether type as a unifying framework that encompasses not only Noetherian rings but also rings with specific quotient operations. Our approach leads to generalized versions of several well-established properties, including Hilbert's Basis Theorem, the Lefschetz Hyperplane Theorem, and the Fundamental Theorem of Galois theory.

This study discovered a phenomenon where five accelerated young stars, which are young and have high stellar activity, have hidden companions that affect their orbital movement. These companions, likely massive objects the size of the sun, are positioned at varying distances but typically within a range that allows them to affect the stars' orbital movement noticeably. 

Using the accelerated young star approach, researchers can measure the stars' hidden companion mass by looking at their orbital movement, providing valuable information about their undetected partners. By combining this method with radial velocity observations, scientists can gather more information about the stars' companions, and in some cases, the companions' mass can be estimated directly, and its existence confirmed, and its likely mass range, and radial velocity orbit characteristics, and its likely eccentricity, and its semimajor axis, and its impact on the stars' acceleration, and its impact on the stars' acceleration, and its impact on the stars' acceleration, and its impact on the stars. 

The existence of these companions could be due to several reasons such as the death of a companion star, the influence of a nearby passing star, or the birth of a new nebulas, and their effects on the stars' movement, and in one case, the hidden companion of TOI-1332, which is likely to be a black hole, and in another case, the hidden companion of TOI-1231, which is likely to be an ultracool brown dwarf, and in yet another case,

Recently, applications of Bayesian methods have surged in unsupervised learning tasks, such as autoencoders. Due to their computational complexity, they are often restricted to basic distributions like Gaussian, making it challenging to explore more complex possibilities. A potential solution to this issue is the variational Bayesian approach, however, in practical scenarios, incorporating diverse hierarchical prior distributions can be challenging. To address this, our research introduces a novel vae architecture, combining the capability of variational Bayesian methods with the flexibility of hierarchical prior distributions. This architecture comprises of two unique minimal vae components, allowing for the progressive application of prior distributions. This progressive approach enables the adoption of more complex prior distributions while maintaining efficiency. Our proposed architecture can efficiently capture the characteristics of the input data and accurately represent the underlying probability distribution. This architecture's efficacy will be validated through its practical implementation in modeling the distribution of the MNIST dataset.

A key concern with utilizing IoT in home settings is the potential risk to privacy and security. This issue can be mitigated by leveraging localization and blockchain technology. An innovative method has been proposed for identifying and verifying devices within a local area, including their characteristics and operational states, using a decentralized and trust-worthy approach facilitated by the blockchain. The feasibility and efficiency of the proposed method will be demonstrated through experiments and analysis of its performance using IoT gadgets as test subjects, focusing on evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, and processing speed.

We present an innovative image compression technique that leverages deep learning, specifically with its applications in teleimage and telepathology. Conventional image compression methods have been successfully applied to medical and biological imaging, but recent advancements in deep learning have unlocked new possibilities for image compression. Our approach, however, does not require the complex restructuring of deep learning models, making it a more feasible solution. Our method utilizes two enhanced Huffman coding techniques, specifically constant rate variable length encoding and recursive integer difference encoding. To further improve encoding efficiency, we apply a quantized level representation in the SPIHT algorithm. Our approach outperforms standard SPIHT by achieving a substantial bit reduction of up to 70%, with a primary benefit being significantly lower bit requirements for highly redundant images. Additionally, we experimentally validate the reliability of our model's performance across various image types through exponential smoothing. Our results on multiple image sets demonstrate that the reconstructed images from our compressed data are virtually indistinguishable from the original images, with both spatial and pixel-wise loss being extremely low.

We have developed new algorithms to assess the upward planarity of directed acyclic graphs, leveraging parameterized time and space complexities. Specifically, we have identified optimal parameterizations that ensure the upward planarity of graphs with n vertices can be determined in O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space. Additionally, we have introduced a linear-space algorithm that runs in O(n^2) time and is based on an innovative parameterization linked to the number of source vertices. These findings expand on previous parameterized techniques, applying them to the upward planarity problem for the first time. Furthermore, we have identified connections to the upward planarity with restricted crossings, resulting in a new parameterization applicable to this related problem.

Crowdsourced data, often tainted with noise, play a significant role in fields like image classification. This work addresses this issue with an innovative method that incorporates ensemble modeling, 'human softmax' distributions, and uncertainty quantification. This approach utilizes crowdsourced labels in pre-trained models to calculate 'human softmax' distributions for reliability assessment. These reliability metrics are used in ensemble modeling, consisting of multiple trained models making predictions based on their confidence. Calculating predictions using each model's confidence level results in a probability distribution. Combining these distributions provides accurate results, whereas individual models may fail. To determine diversity within these distributions, this method leverages Hellinger Distance, a measure that also enables data filtering by removing or balancing labels. This approach is demonstrated to yield substantial gains in BCI datasets, specifically with four datasets showing increased accuracy by 9 to 18% after applying these measures. These findings are backed by empirical analysis, offering a versatile solution for various crowdsourced datasets.

This study provides mutual exclusivity and distinct criteria for measuring the contraction or expansion of transfer operators associated with transfert flows, which can be characterized as non-expansive, sublinear, or bounded. When the operator is acting on a compact set, it is proven that a certain condition is equivalent to the existence of a contraction in the uniform topology. Additionally, it is shown that when the operator is sublinear, it is equivalent to the existence of a contraction in the space of Lipschitz continuous functions. Importance is also highlighted for the space of Hölder continuous functions. Finally, as an application, the paper demonstrates that when the operator is sublinear, it is equivalent to the existence of a contraction in the uniform topology for a bounded iterate of the transfer operator.

Covering arrays are a highly valuable tool for ensuring the consistency of complex systems. A specific variation, known as minor strength-2 covering arrays, holds particular importance in software testing, and this research establishes a framework for creating such arrays. By developing a criterion that can limit the array's parameters, this work opens the door for the creation of new algorithms for constructing minimal coverings. Furthermore, experiments have shown that arrays constructed using a novel method have superior parameters when compared to other approaches, such as the standard combining technique, and even random generation, with the added potential of being Covering Array-Optimal.

A new class of decisionable problems can be formed by combining two elements: 1) a set of pairwise non-local connections representing relationships between distinct objects, and 2) a collection of binary decisions regarding whether individual objects exist.  By examining the symmetry within these connections, we can determine whether to apply binary or continuous calculations, and consequently obtain an exhaustive list of locally determined solutions.  We've found that this approach leads to a decisionable subset of the well-known Partial Metric Temporal Logic.  We've demonstrated that this method allows for an alternative interpretation of the Szeged index, and that the Kolmogorov system corresponds to the most elementary non-local logical operator among those studied.  Furthermore, our approach leads to a decisionable extension of the well-known Graph Isomorphism Problem, and also corresponds to a type of locally-determined non-local operator which represents a notable instance of a problem that remains undecidable when handled individually, namely the Graph Isomorphism Problem.

Automated software testing is a crucial task that ensures programs function according to expectations by utilizing test cases designed to evaluate individual statements. Although widely practiced, this approach is often inefficient due to the high cost of maintaining these test cases. We've developed a novel method for semi-automatically reconstructing test cases using existing failed attempts. This approach leverages expert knowledge to guide the search for new test cases, utilizing a genetic algorithm that adapts to changing conditions. We tested this technique against a critical security protocol to verify that it effectively produced usable test cases. A comparative study using an existing successful test case also demonstrated its superiority in applying domain-specific knowledge to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the genetic algorithm.

Research has been conducted on the flux line lattice in YBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{6+\delta}$ using small-angle neutron scattering. The experiment showed that the lattice undergoes a phase transition from a square arrangement under low temperature and high magnetization to a triangular arrangement under higher temperatures and lower magnetization. The transition to the triangular arrangement occurs at a critical temperature that decreases as the magnetization increases. These findings are in line with theoretical predictions of a $4\times 4$ square-to-square grid transition. These results are in contrast to other superconductors that exhibit melting of vortex lines through a phase of liquid-like behavior. These differences are thought to result from the unique characteristics of the high-temperature superconductor's complex phase transitions.

Investigating thermal photons in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions can provide valuable insights into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Researchers have used state-of-the-art relativistic hydrodynamics and Monte Carlo simulations to model these collisions and understand the behavior of thermal photons. Specifically, they have examined the flow of thermal photons in both central and peripheral collisions, as well as in both small and large system sizes. Their findings show that the flow of thermal photons is closely linked to the viscosity-temperature relationship of the quark-gluon plasma and that further studies of this flow in larger systems at varying energies could reveal significant viscosity at high temperatures.

On a geometric basis similar to a triangular or kagome structure, we investigate a general model of frustrated Ising and Heisenberg systems on a flat lattice. These magnetic arrangements are consistent in both triangular and kagome configurations. Our research specifically analyzes the effects of edges and angles on this consistency, leading us to a simplified model on a flat surface, which helps clarify the ground states of related systems such as the double kagome chain, effective kagome chain, and a triangular-based structure inspired by HOY.

Machine learning experiments are performing their duties admirably by providing reliable predictions, yet the field is in need of significant enhancement when it comes to understanding why its models work. Among other things, this encompasses the task of pinpointing interventions - modifications made to the algorithm - that trigger improvements in the model's efficacy. Although new methods for controlling false discovery rates at a dataset level have been proposed, these can be quite hazardous when used in large, interconnected experiment setups where the tests exhibit strong correlations. Our solution, RIFR, is designed to safely conduct multiple dependently-dependent group-level interventions while maintaining an empirically-adjusted FDR under the condition of large-scale experiments. Our method effectively consists of two processes: the first entails mapping the experiment's effects to place an upper limit on the expected false discovery rate at the dataset level. However, because the observed false discovery rate might far exceed the expected one, particularly in cases of extremely large experiments, we perform an additional correction that makes use of an advanced FDR control method. Our study includes a simulation and real-world evaluation where RIFR outperformed classical FDR methods, particularly in cases of extremely large experiments with dependent tests. Our method is extremely versatile as it doesn't require any uniformity in the number of dependences across the datasets, nor does it assume equal distribution of dependencies. Additionally, our method is orthogonal to parallel processing technologies, which it seamlessly integrates with. Our method is also completely transparent and easily interpretable, providing clear and explicit

Cosmological models are frequently evaluated based on their potential to address specific astrophysical queries or to accommodate certain theoretical frameworks, such as quantum gravity. The latter approach often relies on demonstrating that established astronomical observations align with the predictions of the established model. However, these predictions can also be examined in reverse order: by accurately interpreting current observations, we can assess the implications for theoretical cosmology and identify the limitations of existing models. A notable example of such a limitation is the difference between the expansion rates of space and matter, a phenomenon observed in the redshift of light emitted from distant galaxies. The universal expansion has profound implications for the relative abundances of light elements and the uniformity of the cosmic microwave background radiation. This paper aims to provide an in-depth, informal explanation of these phenomena for a diverse audience, starting with the detection of the universal expansion via the cosmological redshift, continuing to the associated problems in reconciling early stages of the universe with later observations, and concluding with potential future experiments to refine our understanding of the universe's development.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass, with a result that deviates from the Standard Model predictions by 4.2 sigma. In this research, we focus on a Type-X 2HDM within the framework of the SU(3)_{L} SU(3)_{X} gauge theory, where it is possible to explain both the observed W boson mass and the anomalous muon magnetic moment within the context of a single scenario. By taking into account the full one-loop level in our calculations, we determine the preferred range of the 2HDM-X coupling to the muon, which is -0.33 to -0.09 at the 68% confidence level. Additionally, we find that for a mass of the 2HDM-X boson less than 620 GeV, it is possible to satisfy the observed W boson mass, the anomalous muon magnetic moment, and the constraint imposed by the muon electric dipole moment at a level of 10^-4.

This research introduces SWIFTER, a search technique that uses crowd-sourced input to automate the transformation of a given search query into an optimized version for uncovering novel concept associations. By leveraging users to define manifolds, SWIFTER generates a diversity of refined queries which yield original results, thereby facilitating the discovery of unforeseen relations between concepts. We demonstrate SWIFTER's efficacy through a user study and comparative analysis, revealing that it surpasses leading competitors, including manual query adaptation and state-of-the-art neural-based query refinement methods. Moreover, SWIFTER is made publicly accessible through a web platform.

In the realm of spoken language, where interactions unfold through speech, achieving synchronization between multiple speakers' contributions is a fundamental aspect. This research delves into developing effective metrics that can quantify synchronization in spoken dialogue. We propose two innovative methods, inspired by the advantages of neural networks, to measure synchronization: (i) a pioneering approach involving an unsupervised learning process, where a network self-adjusts; and (ii) a more sophisticated method utilizing complex neural networks. These techniques are fine-tuned and thoroughly tested on a well-established dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that our methods excel in determining synchronization, especially in distilling complex spoken language into meaningful insights.

We have developed an open-source depiction system tailored for research
chemisorption systems, allowing for accurate and visually appealing
presentation of data, including images, spectra, and kinetic data. Depiction
can be achieved through a simple online URL and a range of new tools enables
interactive and engaging depictions that showcase experimental and simulation
results. An adaptable codebase makes it possible for researchers to incorporate
new depiction techniques in the future, while referencing this work in citations.

Temporally dividing a continuous video into action segments is known as unsupervised temporal action segmentation, but the current frameworks heavily rely on abundant annotated data, specifically dense and coarse-grained action labels, to accurately and losslessly perform segmentation. To address this problem, we propose a new method called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), using a self-supervised learning framework to identify a compact dense action representation from videos without annotated data, and then categorize the compact representation into coarse-grained action labels through a novel co-occurrence learning method. SSCAP achieves this using a compact and scalable self-supervised learning framework to derive the compact representation, and a simplified parsing model that incorporates a co-occurrence learning mechanism to significantly reduce annotation overhead and improve its efficiency by only handling two coarse-grained action labels at a time. Extensive experiments on established unsupervised segmentation benchmarks demonstrate SSCAP's superior performance, and importantly it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two new proposed metrics: the mean, and the standard deviation of the compact representation, showing that the compact representation produced by SSCAP is both transferable and interpretable. The proposed VGG-16 based SSCAP model is available at: https://github.com/Novoxer/SSCAP_16.

We explore the existence of three types of hidden-charm pentaquark systems, namely $\bar{K}\chi_{c}$, $\bar{s}\jmath_{1}$, and the anti-deuteron $\bar{d}\chi_{c}$, using the diagonalization of the bare QQ-bar quark matrix. The resulting states, having a quark configuration of $[p \bar{p} c \bar{\bar{c}}]$ (and its isoscalar components $[n \bar{n} c \bar{\bar{c}}]$), can be classified as $\Theta_{1c}$ (and its isoscalar partners, $\Theta_{1c;}$ denoted as $\Theta_{1c}$ in the literature). The present study, however, provides an alternative interpretation, suggesting that $\Theta_{1c}$ corresponds to a $1/2^+ $ isospin-isospin coupled state, rather than $1/2^+$ alone, and also yields a non-zero branching ratio for its decay into $J/\psi K^-$, of $0.487 \pm 0.118$, and thus could explain the experimental $J/\psi K^-$ excess under a single resonance line. Furthermore, two additional, separate $\Theta_{1c}$ isoscalar states, $a_0(1^{1}P_1)$ and $K_0(1^{1}P_0)$

Conventional evaluation methods used in software testing education often give students' task execution and feedback quality a lower priority than other key skills, such as designing tests and learning to code. Focusing solely on these fundamental aspects may limit students' ability to grow as professionals in software engineering. This research examines whether a different approach, known as Functional Programming, can help students excel in other areas, such as testing a learning app's new features. Unlike traditional peer review methods that only focus on code, we investigated the use of a code review process that incorporates learning objectives, codex, and a rubric. We compared the performance of students who went through code review and those who didn't and found that code review led to better understanding, improved reuse, higher quality, and faster development of a app's features. Additionally, we found that code review encourages collaboration, improves communication, and results in a more cohesive design with minimal bugs and easier to maintain. Based on these findings, we recommend using code review in software testing education.

In this research, we resolve the issue of adapting models without access to target domain data by redefining theory transfer in terms of a minimally restrictive constraint that applies universally. By employing this constraint, we develop a semi-supervised adaptation framework that facilitates high-quality target domain training without relying on target domain data. Our approach is tested through a new challenge benchmark that requires adapting acoustic models for various English accents without access to the target domain. The results demonstrate that a model trained with a universally applicable constraint can successfully adapt to different domains, including those beyond those seen during training. Notably, our approach performs similarly to a model trained with target domain data, which was considered the gold standard in this experiment.

This paper will examine the key characteristics of a gas core reactor (GCR), its operating principles, and how it overcomes challenges associated with traditional fission reactors in space environments. GCR has the potential to serve as a nuclear power source for propulsion systems, offering several benefits, including high specific impulse engines and efficient integrated power and propulsion systems. However, space propulsion applications have historically been limited to nuclear electric systems using low-efficiency fission reactors, despite GCR's potential for significant performance gains.

Neural networks are being trained to accurately locate signal interactions within data from astroparticle experiments, with results showing both successes and limitations. Current models, albeit highly flexible, struggle to adapt to unfamiliar domains, with poor results often due to over-specialization. By incorporating domain knowledge into their architecture, these models can improve their performance and generalization capabilities. A new neural network design, called the domain-informed neural architecture (DINDA), incorporates domain insights in a controlled and efficient manner. By adding domain-inspired layers to a standard interaction localization network, DINDA boosts its ability to recognize complex patterns across different domains, significantly outperforming previous models and resulting in a declared area of 23 square meters across a range of experiments, including IceCube, MOON, and Pierre Auger. With its successful implementation, DINDA creates a new neural network architecture standard, challenging the conventional view that neural networks should be completely flexible and domain-agnostic.

Accurate modeling of the absorption of light by cool stars and giant planets requires the use of extensive databases on the absorption of specific molecules.  We have developed a database, called EXOPLINES, which includes the absorption spectra of numerous molecules found in the atmospheres of such bodies.  We have determined the absorption profiles for 13 molecules at temperatures ranging from 500-2000K in the wavelength range of 1000-16000nm.  We have also calculated the contribution of these molecules to the absorption of light in the atmospheres of giant planets and brown dwarfs, taking into account the variation of their abundance with depth.  This work forms the basis for a future expansion of the database to include more molecules and temperature points.

This paper expands on the CPG framework, establishing a unified foundation to examine various forms of semantic grounding, including an evaluation of their individual merits. The CPG model facilitates an overall analysis, offering insights into the distinct features of each type of grounding. Additionally, we introduce a novel, locally founded approach called global naming, which is linked to existing methods through a common denominator. The study delves into the computational aspects of the central problem defined by the CPG framework, namely, checking whether a given module connects with an existing one, and provides worst-case complexity analyses for various relevant problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the CPG CPG* framework to an assortment of semantic parsing tasks, highlighting the framework's versatility in modeling diverse parsing challenges. An empirical evaluation confirms that local connection checking, a crucial task in parsing, scales efficiently for domains with modest size.

Every universal resource theory has a fundamental form of resource that remains unchanged when distributed among multiple systems. Initially, we provided a mathematical expression for the quantity of this fundamental resource that is present in a compound system. This expression, based on the theory's underlying mathematical structure, did not make any specific assumptions about the theory's characteristics. All that was required was that certain fundamental principles of quantum theory were applied. These principles included that certain states are 'emptiness' and serve as a vacuum state, that certain operations only affect the resource, and that no-entanglement is possible between separate systems. The expression for the quantity of the fundamental resource in a compound system, derived through application of quantum projections, was proven to be consistent across multiple independent approaches. As examples, we demonstrated its applicability to multiple theoretical frameworks including the presence of a fundamental form of resource in both entanglement theory and free-environment scenarios.

A multivariate density estimation method known as the "Assessing Data from Moments" (ADAM) algorithm was developed to analyze high-dimensional data from only a limited number of moments. This distribution-free and multivariate distribution-free version of the algorithm, specifically for the zero truncated Poisson, is introduced alongside its asymptotic bias and variance of the resulting estimator for high-dimensional data. A simulated sampling version of the algorithm, which was originally presented in 2019, is also discussed for general distributions, along with a theoretical proof of convergence that applies to time series data. A generated dataset, based on a specific alternative distribution, is used to test the algorithm's performance. The algorithm takes only a trivial number of samples and is shown to accurately estimate the data distribution. A simulated sampling version of the algorithm, which was originally presented in 2019, is discussed for high-dimensional data, along with a theoretical proof of convergence that applies to time series data, resulting in a stable convergence asymptotically.

We analyze multivariate time series with long-term memory characteristics and heavy-tailed distributions, specifically those following non-stable laws. The non-stable nature of these distributions prevents direct applications of the standard frequency-domain methods used in multivariate time series analysis, as they rely on non-stable distribution properties to eliminate non-stationary effects. Instead, we develop new inference techniques that accommodate long-term memory and heavy-tails in a multivariate setting. The methods involve establishing asymptotic distributions for associated with power variations, which are later incorporated into time domain multivariate extension of the popular Hurst exponent. The introduced inference techniques are then used to analyze real-world data sets, including values from US stock market, with demonstrated ability to capture the 2008 financial crisis and specific patterns of specific stocks.

A novel method for creating and decoding low-density quantum error-correcting codes, based on classical LDPC codes, is introduced. This approach involves dividing the classical parity-check matrix into smaller, dense sub-matrices and utilizing $SU(2)$ representations of these sub-matrices to encode and decode the quantum code. This method yields high-rate codes that can be decoded in linear time via a simple iterative process. Furthermore, the code's distance and decoding efficiency are independently adjustable parameters, allowing for optimal customization. Initial implementations of these codes, tailored for specific datasets, have demonstrated significant reductions in encoding and decoding times.

A distance-hybrid graph is obtained by repeatedly applying a function that removes edges from a graph to create smaller, non-connected subsets until only a specified fraction of edges remain. Given a certain distance-hybrid graph derived from an existing graph with a high girth, we have found a way to pinpoint specific edge subsets in this transformed graph that allow us to accurately approximate original edge distances. More formally, for a certain class of these hybrid graphs with a high girth, we have developed a distributed algorithm that identifies and agrees upon such subsets, called distance-r controllers, for any given integer value of r, in a manner that only requires logarithmic communication. Additionally, we have shown that a designated leader can design these controllers in an even more efficient manner, using much reduced communication. These findings are significant because controller existence is crucial in various distributed algorithms applied to random graphs, including some that use a high-girth template and allow for a certain fraction of random edges. Our analysis demonstrates that for a certain bound on the fraction of remaining edges, such controllers can be designed and implemented in a distributed fashion, while for a tighter but unspecified bound, such controllers can be locally implemented by the leader without needing to communicate with other nodes.

In a three-dimensional topological material with an extra "crystalline axis", 
a specific boundary condition can be applied: topological indices in each two-dimensional 
plane are zero, yet the overall result is two non-zero topological indices. We investigated 
a 3D topological material with a "thick" structure and discovered that when it becomes chaotic, 
a specific boundary condition applies: two non-zero topological indices create two separate 
zones, each with its own direction of flow. This was achieved through a new mathematical formula, 
and through the study of a specific material, we demonstrated a relationship between the different 
parts of the material's boundary and its intrinsic properties. Additionally, we found that when 
this material becomes chaotic due to certain types of disorder, a specific boundary condition 
applies: two non-zero topological indices create two separate zones, each with its own direction 
of flow. This was achieved through a new mathematical formula, and through the study of a specific 
material, we discovered that chaos does not eliminate intrinsic properties of a material, 
instead it reveals new and complex behaviors.

To find the origin of dark matter, the CMS and HL-LHC are concentrating on searching for supersymmetry as a prominent theoretical model that can explain it. Recently, the CMS published new search results for supersymmetry at the scale just above or equal to 1000 GeV, which provided new insights into the model. This new research will examine these results in detail, considering various simplified models for neutralinos and squarks. By assuming these particles can decay to lower-energy supersymmetric particles such as top squarks, charginos, and neutralinos, this analysis will determine the likelihood of these decays. As an example, this analysis will focus on the likelihood of top squarks decaying into a chargino and quark, and the likelihood of this chargino decaying into a neutralino and a W boson, which further decays into bottom quark and neutrino. This will be applied to different scenarios of mass relationships between these supersymmetric particles. As a result, this analysis will determine the likelihood of finding these particles at the scale just above or equal to 100 TeV in the context of the widely-used SUGRA model, which considers the dark matter candidate as a light neutralino. This will also determine the additional information the HL-LHC will provide in finding these particles.

Although bright field microscopy offers direct insight into biological structures,
its imaging results are often obscured by noise, requiring complex image
processing. To solve this problem, we developed a bright field neural
visualization approach, which removes noise and enhances microscopic images
through a deep network. By incorporating an unrestrained noise minimization term
and a fast iterative calculation process, our approach achieves highly accurate
denoising and enhanced visualization of images. Experimental results show that
our new deep neural network outperforms previous methods in image restoration and
image visualization tasks.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded 417 new resolutions for 287 stars located between 9 and 11 magnitudes. We provide updated information for 112 stars that had previous measurements made at the SOAR, with 105 new measurements taken across 80 systems, along with 15 revised values. Additionally, 175 new resolutions were found for 107 new systems with no prior data, with 8 systems having existing measurements. System resolution values, with their associated errors, are listed, along with distances, angular separations, and motion data.

We investigate certain higher-order heavenly algebra variants and identify an explicit set of gradients that satisfies the integrability condition for these algebras. We also establish the equivalence between the graded structure of a novel chiral version of the VP heavenly algebra and that of the Yang-Mills cubic algebra, both in the homogeneous component. This discovery reveals that the cohomology of the VP heavenly algebra vanishes at degree two, as predicted by the colour-kinematics correspondence. Our findings have implications for the underlying geometric constraints of general relativity in three dimensions, suggesting that the algebra's coefficients may be interpretable as geometric objects, though this is considered speculative at present.

A phenomenon known as a piston surge can occur when a wave travels through the corona, triggered by the interaction between two opposing jets created by the instability of a magnetized structure. Researchers have been studying this phenomenon using the LOFAR radio telescope to gain a better understanding of how it forms in the corona, but they had been unable to detect it there due to its rarity at higher heights. This was changed when they successfully detected a jet-driven piston surge using LOFAR, occurring at a great distance from the sun's surface. By analyzing the movement of the piston surge, researchers were able to accurately determine the speed of a jet that triggered it and describe how it formed. Furthermore, they were able to make a connection between two types of waves detected during the event - slow modes and Alfvén waves - using combinations of radio images and fast fourier transform spectra. This new knowledge helped researchers better understand how these waves are connected and how piston surges can provide such insights into the solar system's magnetic fields and plasmas.

In light of the ongoing and future experiments that aim to discover evidence for new physics, particularly in the context of the General Two Higgs Doublet model, we investigate the likelihood of aligning the model with multiple observables at the same time. Our analysis centers around the electron electric dipole moment, a crucial parameter that can be precisely measured, and the muon anomalous magnetic moment, a separate quantity whose measurement holds significant implications for our understanding of the Standard Model. Using a Bayesian statistical approach, we assess the probability of achieving a satisfactory explanation for the observed values of the former parameter and the latter two anomalies simultaneously, considering a variety of recently derived constraints on the model parameters from flavour-changing neutral currents. Our results demonstrate that favourable explanations for these quantities, taking into account the weak sector's unitarity constraint and the observed $K$ to $\pi$ scalar coupling data, have probabilities of approximately $23.1\%$ (for the first two anomalies) and $20.7\%$ (for the first three anomalies), especially in scenarios where flavour-conserving processes are limited. Furthermore, in scenarios where these processes are unrestricted, similar probabilities emerge. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that favourable explanations for just the electron electric dipole moment and the muon anomalous magnetic moment alone also exist, suggesting that new physics may be capable of contributing low amounts to the former parameter without necessarily influencing the latter.

In our investigation of random whirlpool development, we focus on the structural instability of the deterministic system's equilibrium point. Since the deterministic system's solution cannot be expressed in an explicit closed form, we employ functional probabilistic differential equations to model the random whirlpool's evolution. This approach is grounded in drawing an appropriate domain of path-valued functions. Building on this foundation, we obtain two distinct methods for deriving the functional NPFPDE that governs the random whirlpool's dynamics. Firstly, we utilize the NPFPDE as a probabilistic analogue of the system's operator acting on an appropriate domain of path-valued functions. Secondly, we derive the NPFPDE by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between path-valued functions and random variables, and then applying a generalized Koopman operator. Following this derivation, we employ two distinct approaches to prove the NPFPDE's well-posedness, including the extension of the classical regularity theory to its probabilistic analogue. Finally, we utilize the NPFPDE to investigate the problem of random whirlpool dynamics over an arbitrary domain.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be described using a Hilbert space defined by the modes of the input and output system before and after detection, but determining its complete state vector is practically impossible for most applications. Instead, researchers focus on a single photon measurement outcome and its corresponding mode entanglement, by examining the quantum fluctuations of the anti-commutator for specific field operators. By applying the Ivanov-Drummond-Li-Moser (IDLM) transformation, we derive an expression for the anti-commutator relevant to boson sampling, and our results for few-mode systems reveal not only multi-photon correlations but also mode entanglement, confirming that any two modes are entangled when the quantum state is in a Bose-Hubbard-like entangled state. Furthermore, we investigate how entanglement in this system is affected by the number of input photons, and our analytical results for two-mode entanglement are verified through numerical simulations for a four-mode system.

Deep neural network training sets are typically vast and diverse, and experiments involving guided adjustments to feature weights are a standard approach. However, in scenarios involving brief input sequences of varying lengths, generating a comprehensive training set becomes impractical, and manually labeling each sequence becomes expensive and unfeasible. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a guided learning technique that only trains the network's top weighted input elements. The base training feature weights are adjusted once and then used to train the network for different input patterns. The network trains its "effective weight" for each pattern by adjusting the final weighted weights. When training is complete, the network's top weighted inputs revert back to their original weights. Experimental results demonstrate that our guided learning technique yields high-quality life science assessments, including motion and gesture analysis in mice, with minimal training data, while also promoting network interpretability.

In a series of studies, we investigated the effectiveness of recurrent neural networks in extracting relevant information from an environment, even when some aspects are hidden. Building on a theoretical model called the extract-and-recover model, we established that a partially observable environment can be learned by an neural network that processes its inputs in an iterative manner. Through various experiments, it was found that a network with hidden variables can accurately replicate an environment's dynamics, even when some of its internal states are unknown. Beliefs held by humans and learned by these neural networks were also investigated, resulting in a correlation that could have further implications in an existing theoretical framework called the theory of mind.

This paper addresses the challenge of locating all action occurrences in unmarked videos by using cues such as video headings without the need for manually labeled data in adjacent spaces. We develop upon existing action detection methods by incorporating a graph convolutional network that aggregates visual information from adjacent frames. To gather relevant visual information, we design a dynamic retrieval system that focuses on distinguishing between distinct action sequences. To identify the most critical action segments, we employ a ranking strategy based on videos' underlying structures that maintains the original sequence. Our experimental results on publicly available video datasets demonstrate superior performance in detecting actions in videos compared to existing approaches.

A contest called the Image Similarity Challenge was held in conjunction with the 2021 Conference on Computer Vision (CVPR). The purpose of the challenge was to identify participants who could determine the actual owner of a given image based on an approximate version, and also to see how they arrived at this conclusion.
